articles.title_orig: China can lead APEC by example
articles.title_zh: China can lead APEC by example
articles.content_orig:
Peer reviewed analysis from world leading experts
The Australian National University
As the US retreats from the global trading rules it once underwrote, the 18–19 November 2026 APEC summit in Shenzhen gives China a chance to present itself as a credible defender of multilateralism. But it should not define that role against Washington. China can make its case for APEC leadership by running open and inclusive meetings, developing transparency norms to security-justified trade measures and pursuing domestic reform, including by upholding its WTO commitments and making visible progress towards CPTPP standards.
The 18–19 November 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen is the third time China has hosted the summit and the first since the United States retreated from the global trading rules it once underwrote. Domestic commentary casts China as having moved from participant to leader in APEC. With Washington raising tariffs by executive decision, China can play the part of defender of multilateralism convincingly.
The mistake would be to define that role against the United States and leave Washington out of the community the summit is meant to build. Open regionalism was designed in part to keep the United States engaged while East Asia integrated, with member economies opening on a non-discriminatory basis and bound by the same disciplines. A summit framed solely in terms of contest with Washington would also make it harder for middle powers to back China’s agenda, since most want to avoid choosing sides and prefer to rely on rules-based protections.
China can make its case for APEC leadership most effectively through its conduct in three areas.
The first is how it runs the ministerial and leaders’ meetings. As APEC decides by consensus and enforces nothing, much of its work depends on informal contact. The leaders’ retreat has shaped APEC’s direction since 1993, and sideline meetings have produced breakthroughs. Notable cases include the 1999 US–China discussion that restarted China’s World Trade Organization accession talks and the 2025 trade truce agreed to by US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
China proposed a leaders’ program without a retreat , with the foreign and trade ministers meeting online rather than in person on 3 November 2026. Keeping the retreat would give accompanying ministers time to meet in person and leave room for sideline meetings among all 21 members. APEC’s results come from these unscripted exchanges and a host that wants to lead the forum should accept the risks that come with them.
The second area is the boundary between security and trade. Export controls , investment screening and subsidies justified on security grounds have become the main ways security concerns are shaping trade policy. APEC could develop norms of transparency, notification and consultation that make it easier to tell a security measure from protection in disguise. China has a strong interest in such norms, since its firms are the main target of other members’ controls and screening.
But others are unlikely to accept them unless China applies them to its own measures first, including its rare earth export controls. China has the strongest case for its measures when they are confined to clearly defined military end uses and affected partners are notified. Since China tightened controls on exports to Japan in January 2026, other economies have been watching how they are applied to judge whether China keeps security and trade apart.
The same restraint matters for what follows the US–China truce, now extended to 10 January 2027. Other members are concerned about the next round of arrangements, which may be agreed upon in Shenzhen. Open regionalism suggests how China can keep such arrangements from coming at its partners’ expense. Beijing should extend to all APEC members any market opening or export-control relief it agrees with Washington and consult affected partners before taking on purchase commitments.
China’s APEC leadership will also be judged by its own reform. At Osaka in 1995, China pledged to cut its average tariffs by at least 30 per cent without asking for reciprocal concessions. It implemented the cuts at home and later locked them in through its accession to the WTO. Xi’s pledge in Shenzhen on 18 November 2026 to move towards reforming rules, regulations and standards is the first step in the same sequence, which can be completed at the WTO and in China’s bid to join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP).
Premier Li Qiang announced in September 2025 that China would not seek new special and differential treatment at the WTO. But the 2026 Yaounde WTO ministerial conference ended without a reform work program and the moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions lapsed in March 2026 . Leaders in Shenzhen could commit to keep electronic transmissions duty-free and China could add transparency commitments on subsidies and state-owned enterprises.
China applied to join the CPTPP in 2021, but progress has been slow. Members have yet to open an accession working group and the case for the bid is still being debated in China. Seven of the CPTPP’s 12 members are already in RCEP with China and the United States is not a party.
These doubts overlook what the bid can do before accession. An application signals political will, while domestic reforms demonstrate commitment prior to accession. Visible progress on members’ main concerns would make CPTPP standards a benchmark for reforms that would benefit China anyway.
A reform package foreshadowed in Shenzhen and delivered at Vietnam’s 2027 APEC summit would be the clearest evidence of China’s openness. The most immediate concern for China’s partners is its surging exports and weak consumption. The shift towards household demand set out in the 15th Five-Year Plan is the right way to address the source of that imbalance, which trade rules alone cannot resolve .
Other members have a part to play too. CPTPP members, who meet in Vietnam in November 2026, could set out a process in which China advances as it demonstrates reform, so that decisions turn on standards rather than geopolitics.
Shenzhen’s success will depend not only on the US–China meeting, but also on how the leaders’ and ministerial meetings are run, how the boundary between trade and security is navigated, and how China carries out domestic reforms. Progress in these areas would do more to shore up regional support for the multilateral system than any statement the summit issues.
Patrick Xue is Research Scholar at the East Asian Bureau of Economic Research in the Crawford School of Public Policy, The Australian National University.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Falls as Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors' Nerves
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Falls as Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors' Nerves
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares declined another 2.89% Wednesday after the company issued its first earnings report since the departure of former CEO Jensen Huang . The stock is down more than 13% over the past week.
Trading in the neocloud companies was volatile throughout the day, as CoreWeave closed down 4.13%, Iren sank 3.61% and Nebius whipsawed, ending the trading day up 0.87%.
Nvidia's third-quarter revenue came in at $115.84 billion, more than $6 billion above analysts' expectations of $109.10 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion topped the $125.1 billion consensus, according to LSEG.
The semiconductor giant continues to navigate the fallout from Huang's resignation last week. Shortly before the results, Huang made his first public statement since resigning last week, saying that he was open to returning to the company, after an outpouring of support from prominent tech figures .
But Harvey Jones, the new and first-ever chair of Nvidia's board, said on the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate him as CEO.
″[Hyperscalers] are the ones that are right now feverishly looking for more focus in terms of the compute that we have available," interim CEO Colette Kress told Jim Cramer on CNBC's "Mad Money."
"This concept that anything is changing in terms of any of our types of customers — that is just not true. They are all continuing to be with us, and we have a very deep breath of different customers."
The U.S. Commerce Department announced a legal change on Monday to try and stem China's access to the most advanced Nvidia chips — which are already under export controls effectively preventing their import into the country — by restricting Chinese companies' ability to access compute remotely in overseas data centers.
In a letter Wednesday, the House Energy and Commerce Committee asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear to discuss chip export controls, and requested a briefing from interim CEO Colette Kress by Dec. 2.
Nvidia told investors in its earnings commentary that it was "not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in our outlook," in keeping with its recent language on the country.
Huang is slated to appear before several Congressional committees in the coming weeks.
Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box" Wednesday, Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Huang and Lutnick have agreed to appear before the committee in December. It's slated to be Huang's second appearance on Capitol Hill in December, after the former Nvidia CEO reached an agreement with three House committees to appear for closed-door interviews on Dec. 1.
— CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: What the Crimean bridge attack means for Russia
articles.title_zh: What the Crimean bridge attack means for Russia
articles.content_orig:
It had been a year and a half since Ukraine last attacked the 19-kilometer-long Kerch Bridge connecting Russian-annexed Crimea with Russia's Krasnodar region.
Now, Ukraine has struck again. The attack during the night of November 17 caused the highway section of the bridge to collapse into the sea. As a result, shipping traffic between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov has also been disrupted.
Russia's ministry of transport announced a "temporary suspension" of road and rail traffic on the bridge, though later, rail services were resumed. Russian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into what they are calling a "terrorist attack." It was only after this announcement that the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) confirmed the attack.
The Kerch Strait bridge is considered one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prestigious projects. Its construction began after Russia's 2014 annexation of the Ukrainian Crimea peninsula , an act considered illegal under international law. The Kerch Bridge was completed four years later.
It has been targeted by Ukraine on several occasions since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion . The most well-known strike occurred in October 2022, when an explosives-laden truck detonated on the bridge, causing extensive damage and several months of traffic restrictions. The most recent attack took place in June 2025, when the SBU reported that an underwater support structure was blown up.
The latest Ukrainian operation lasted about a month, and consisted of seven distinct phases. "First, the SBU and armed forces systematically neutralized the enemy's air defense system. After that, the direct attack on the bridge began," says the SBU Telegram channel.
Some Russian military bloggers claim that the attack was carried out with the support of Ukraine's Western allies, or at least using their equipment and weapons.
Ukraine has not confirmed this. It has instead pointed out that various Ukrainian-made weapons were used in the attack, ranging from a variety of drones, to FP-5 Flamingo and R-360 Neptun missiles. British daily The Times has cited Ukrainian military sources, saying that Ukraine attacked the bridge without the support of SpaceX's satellite network system Starlink . There has been no confirmation of this so far.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , meanwhile, described the strike as a response to Russian attacks: "Russia is attacking our infrastructure every day, particularly bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region." He said "we are rebuilding our infrastructure, but we also remind Russia that the war always returns to where it began."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
After the attack, pictures and videos of the bridge were shared on social media. The Krimskij Veter Telegram channel has highlighted damage to the railroad link and questioned why Russian authorities have opted to resume train services.
The Kerch Strait shipping channel is also completely blocked by debris. "This brings road traffic to a standstill, but also shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov," the channel writes.
Indeed, the Kerch Strait navigational channel is merely 120 meters wide, writes Mychajlo Hontschar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" on Facebook. "The strait is shallow, only three to five meters deep."
As early as the 19th century, the seabed was dredged to allow heavier ships to pass from the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov and vice versa. "Now, Vladimir Putin's bridge-building efforts have brought shipping to an indefinite standstill," Hontschar said.
Not only will river-sea vessels no longer be able to leave the waters of the Sea of Azov, the Don, and the Volga, but boats and small ships from the Black Sea fleet and the Caspian flotilla based in Novorossiysk will also be unable to do so.
Many pro-Kremlin Telegram channels have been quick to claim that the bridge does not play an important role in the Russian army's logistics or in supplying Crimea.
The Dva Mayora (Two Majors) channel quotes the "Deputy President of the Republic of Crimea," Olga Kurlayeva, who described the bridge as a "purely civilian structure."
Ukrainian military experts interviewed by DW, on the other hand, point to the systematic disruption of Russian logistics. These efforts also included regular attacks on the R-80 highway leading through Russian-occupied territories of the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions.
Russia cannot replace the Kerch Bridge with any other land connection, says Oleksandr Kovalenko, a Ukrainian military expert with the Information Resistance Group that seeks to counter disinformation. He expects the damaged bridge will cause supply problems for the Russian armed forces: "If there is a resource shortage during attacks or in defense, then either the attacks or the defense will fail."
That is why he does not rule out a decline in attacks from occupied Crimea on the rest of Ukraine. "There are many launch pads for kamikaze drones in Crimea — in the Hvardijsk area, at Cape Chauda and in Balaklava," Kovalenko told DW. "From there, many drones are launched toward Odesa, Mykolaiv, and the right bank of the Dnipro River in the Kherson region. They also fly over Crimea en route toward Ukraine. Then there are attacks using Iskander-M ballistic missiles, as well as Zircon and Oniks missiles, guided missiles, and glide bombs. And while they don't originate in Crimea, they are brought over via the Kerch Bridge."
Kovalenko says the bridge strike has dealt a serious blow to Vladimir Putin's standing. It comes at a sensitive time as Putin is about to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Shenzhen, China .
Memes and witty comments about the bridge abound on X. Meanwhile, the Russian president's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has promised to rebuild the bridge and assured that it will be "even better than before."
Andrii Korezkyj of the Kyiv University of Transportation, however, says this is not likely to happen anytime soon. "All in all, I would estimate that it would take between one and a half and three years [to rebuild]," Korezkyj told DW, adding, "I don't think they'll let the Russians build another [bridge] arch like that near the Ukrainian border without interference."
Pro-Russian commentators, known as Z-bloggers, agree with this view. "Unlike in 2022 and 2023, the Ukrainian armed forces are now able to launch strikes against floating cranes and repair teams."
"Even installing a pre-assembled arch under these conditions would constitute a challenging task," writes the pro-Kremlin Rybar Telegram channel.

articles.title_orig: US Stock Futures Rally as Nvidia Results Ease AI Trade Worries
articles.title_zh: US Stock Futures Rally as Nvidia Results Ease AI Trade Worries
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks closed mixed on Wednesday after a turbulent start to the week as Nvidia ( NVDA ) cleared its earnings bar and investors awaited the next big AI catalyst: Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) IPO. Initial reports after the closing bell stated the AI lab has set its share price at $83, above its initial range.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell more than 1.1%. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) slipped 0.2%, while the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) gained 0.4% following two straight days of declines.
Markets wavered after Nvidia reported its first earnings s ince Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO, demonstrating that the AI chip king can continue to deliver a quarter as good as any, even with a scandal overhang. Revenue surged 103% year over year, and the board said it would not reinstate Huang.
Nvidia stock notched its fifth day of losses, while other semiconductor names were mixed.
Anthropic is expected to announce its initial public offering price this evening, initiating what is anticipated to be one of the largest public debuts on Thursday. Here's everything you need to know ahead of Anthropic's IPO .
On the earnings calendar, Target ( TGT ) quarterly results smashed expectations , while Home Depot's counterpart, Lowe's ( LOW ), also beat Wall Street estimates on Wednesday.
Wall Street is already reacting to Anthropic's reported IPO pricing as a positive sign for the tech trade, at a time when investors have been nervous about the sector amid AI chip giant Nvidia's ( NVDA ) recent woes.
Following the market close on Wednesday, Bloomberg reported that the AI lab priced its IPO at $83 per share, well above its $70-78 range.
"Anthropic's IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," said Yorkville's Dan Ives on Wednesday evening.
"It is going through a very turbulent, white-knuckle period that does not change our longer-term view that $3 trillion to $4 trillion of capex will be spent over the next few years on the AI Revolution, and this sets the stage for the next phase of tech and infrastructure investment with Anthropic a central player in the buildout," he added.
Anthropic has reportedly priced its IPO at $83 per share, according to Bloomberg. The outlet, citing people familiar with the matter, said the size of the offering has increased.
The reported price is above the initial $70 to $78 range outlined in the company's filing.
The shares are expected to be priced Wednesday and begin trading on the Nasdaq Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT.
US stocks were mixed on Wednesday as the market shifted its focus to Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) IPO in what could be a major test for the AI trade. Investors expected the AI lab to price its public debut on Wednesday evening, with shares trading on Thursday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) dropped more than 1.1%. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) slipped 0.2%, while the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) gained roughly 0.4%.
Nvidia stock notched its fifth day of losses following better-than-expected quarterly results. The quarter wasn't enough to quell investor worries over leadership changes following Jensen Huang's resignation last week and increasing scrutiny over the company.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock hit session lows in afternoon trading, falling more than 3%. The stock lost its early trading gains following the AI chip giant's better-than-expected quarter and outlook raise amid a tumultuous leadership change.
Wall Street analysts appeared relieved that the company was able to beat expectations and raise its outlook, as it typically does, even after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last Thursday following reports of extramarital affairs, including an alleged relationship with a woman reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.
In the interim, CFO Colette Kress is serving as CEO until a permanent replacement is named.
"While it may be premature to sound the all-clear, NVDA's earnings call was very reassuring as the company, under Interim CEO Kress, appears to be pulling together strongly in defiance of the skeptics," BofA analysts said in a note Wednesday. The analysts reiterated their Buy rating and $280 price target.
However, they noted that the CEO transition could take time and pointed to another unusual development: Nvidia delayed filing its 10-Q, which typically provides more detailed financial disclosures.
In its earnings materials, Nvidia said, "We plan to file our 10-Q in the coming weeks." The company typically files the document alongside its quarterly earnings release.
Yahoo Finance's Pras Subramanian reports:
Ford ( F ) announced on Wednesday that the first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells are coming off the line at its BlueOval Battery Park Michigan, as part of a plan to license China's CATL battery designs. The move comes against the complicated backdrop of using Chinese tech in US made components.
The batteries are headed to Ford's Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky to power prototypes of the Fathom, Ford's upcoming midsize electric pickup. Ford hopes to build an EV cheap enough to win over gas truck buyers, with the Fathom set to start under $30,000 - and key to that is using lower-cost batteries.
"Ford is officially in the battery business. We'll be the first to deliver LFP batteries in the US for mainstream consumer automotive use, and I couldn't be prouder of the Ford team," CEO Jim Farley said on X .
Federal Reserve governor Chris Waller said Wednesday that if the central bank hikes interest rates by a quarter point next month, Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger reports, it will need to signal that the Fed will hike again by that much in January.
"People have argued, do you do 50 in December, nothing in January, or 25 in December, 25 in January," Waller said in an interview Wednesday on CNBC. "But when you do 25 now and you're going to do 25 in January, it only affects market pricing if you signal you're going to do it, and you give the markets a credible signal."
Waller said that if you leave the market guessing about a January rate increase, there won't be an effect on the market and, by extension, the economy.
"If you're not going to signal this very clearly to markets you're going in January, my view is then you have to go 50 in December," Waller said.
The majority of of traders (69%) expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by 50 basis points by the end of January, up from roughly a third (38%) a month ago, according to CME's Fedwatch tool .
Yahoo Finance's Dan Howley reports:
Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) will begin publicly trading Thursday, providing insights into the market's appetite for access to one of the most prominent artificial intelligence labs in the world.
The firm, which will trade under the ticker ANT, says it expects to price shares at between $70 and $78. That would value the company at between $1.3 trillion and $1.45 trillion.
OpenAI CEO and co-founder Sam Altman said Wednesday that the ChatGPT maker is still planning to become a public company as rival Anthropic moves to the final stages of its Thursday listing.
"We plan to be public," Altman said at the New York Times DealBook Summit, adding that there are "many reasons why that's the right thing to do."
Altman said in September during an interview with Fortune that the company would not pursue an initial public offering in 2026 after reports that the major AI startup was going to try.
Anthropic, which was formed by former OpenAI employees and has taken a more concerted effort targeting business customers with its Claude AI tool suite, is expected to begin trading as a public company on Thursday in what could become the largest IPO ever.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration says it's weighing new penalties against China over jailed Americans - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Trump administration says it's weighing new penalties against China over jailed Americans - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Beijing has shut down attempts to open negotiations, officials say.
As President Donald Trump makes a high-stakes visit to China, U.S. officials told ABC News his administration says it's evaluating options aimed at pressuring Beijing to free two American citizens wrongfully detained in the country on allegations of espionage.
Trump has raised the cases of Youlin Chen, a Boston-based seismologist, and Min Zin, a doctoral candidate at University of California, Berkeley, in previous engagements with China’s President Xi Jinping, but the Chinese government has not seriously engaged in any negotiations for their release, according to the officials.
A likely next move would be elevating the State Department’s travel advisory level for China, a diplomatic consequence that can have chilling effect on travel and tourism, U.S. officials told ABC News.
A significantly more severe penalty would be designating China as a State Sponsor of Wrongful Detention , a measure that opens up a range of punitive measures the U.S. government can opt to employ, including financial sanctions and visa restrictions. The officials did not indicate the administration was ready to take that step yet, but said the option remains on the table.
The officials also said the administration would likely wait to take any action until sometime after the president returns from Asia, in order to give talks space to progress.
“We do not preview potential designations or changes to travel advisories,” a State Department spokesman said. “We will continue to evaluate the risks facing Americans in China and take appropriate steps to protect U.S. citizens.”
The president indicated earlier this month he intended to talk to Xi about Americans detained in China during their meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen, China on Thursday.
“I do talk to him about that a lot. And we've done well,” Trump told reporters on Nov. 6 in West Palm Beach, Florida.
The State Department added a wrongful detention risk indicator to its travel advisory for mainland China in October, a move one official said was intended to both alert Americans to potential danger and warn Beijing that additional repercussions were on the horizon.
China’s foreign ministry has repeatedly rejected the State Department’s determination that Chen and Zin and wrongfully detained and maintains that Chinese judicial authorities are handling the cases in accordance with the country’s laws.
Under China’s sweeping national security laws, routine research and data collection may be interpreted as a threat to the country’s interests – putting academics at greater risk of wrongful detention, according to the State Department.
Critics of the Chinese government also say that its national security laws enable the Chinese Communist Party to target foreign nationals involved with topics it deems politically sensitive.
The policy is seemingly at odds with Beijing’s push to expand tourism and academic exchanges with foreign institutions, including those in the U.S. Following a visit to Washington in September , Xi announced a new initiative to invite 100,000 young Americans to study in China over five years.
The U.S. government has determined that the allegations against both Chen and Zin are meritless and classified both men as wrongfully detained.
Chen was detained in 2024 by state security agents during a trip to visit family members in China. Authorities charged him with espionage and are currently holding him in pre-trial detention.
Zin traveled to China to attend an academic conference at Beijing’s invitation in June. Upon his arrival, he was arrested on suspicion of engaging in espionage. He has not yet been formally charged.
While Chen and Zin are the only Americans officially labeled as wrongfully detained by the Chinese government, experts estimate that dozens of Americans in China are subject to exit bans or other coercive measures that limit their ability to leave the country.
Trump is expected to meet face-to-face with Xi at least one more time this year when G20 leaders gather in Miami for the group’s annual summit in December.
“I’ve been assured that President Trump remains firmly committed to securing Youlin’s freedom and that he intends to raise Youlin’s case with President Xi at both the APEC meeting and, if needed, the G20,” Chen’s wife, Yufang Chen, said in a statement to ABC News.
“We all know that when President Trump gets involved, Americans come home,” she added.
Sylvia Zin, Min Zin’s wife, told ABC News she recently learned her husband was hospitalized last month for severe dehydration and that there is no heat at the location where he is being held.
"My worry for my husband's health and wellbeing increases with each passing day,” she said in a statement. "My daughter and I remain hopeful in the President's ability to bring him home to us in time for the holidays."
An ABC News request to the Chinese Embassy for comment on Zin’s status and medical condition did not immediately receive a response.

articles.title_orig: ‘An absolute nightmare’ — Trump’s trilateral with Xi and Putin spooks allies
articles.title_zh: ‘An absolute nightmare’ — Trump’s trilateral with Xi and Putin spooks allies
articles.content_orig:
It’s fine for presidents to meet leaders of US adversaries. But Donald Trump’s summits with authoritarians are so odd because he treats them as friends.
This jarring dynamic may reemerge in his landmark summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in southern China on Thursday. He hopes to complete a trifecta of tyrant check-ins by also meeting with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.
The symbolism of the three-way talks in Shenzhen is stark. Three great powers, each of which stakes a hegemonic claim in its wider geographical orbit, will send a signal of dominance that deliberately excludes smaller, weaker nations.
The optics would be less striking if Trump acted as the leader of the free world facing down ruthless strongmen. But the president shows contempt for US allies and admires the iron rule of Xi and Putin. He frequently excuses their conduct or seeks to avoid upsetting them.
Before leaving for Asia, he argued that Putin — who is raining drones and missiles on Ukrainian civilians — was showing restraint and could be a “lot tougher.” Trump also explained he wasn’t confronting Beijing over an espionage drama involving advanced semiconductor chips because “I don’t think you want to insult China just before you get there.”
There is a fine line between talking with US enemies and appeasing them. The Shenzhen summit may test the boundaries between useful diplomacy to lower superpower tensions and dictator role-playing between two strongmen and an American president who’d like to be one.
Critics fault Trump’s relish for pomp over substance. He basks in flattery from shrewd interlocutors keen to manipulate him. His summits with Xi, Putin and Kim in his first term looked great but delivered little.
Breakthroughs are not expected in Shenzhen. Trump says the leaders might discuss nuclear weapons, Iran and Ukraine. But he’s got little patience for the painstaking prep and intense consultations with allies that predated President Ronald Reagan’s Cold War summits with the last Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev.
“Is this meeting with Putin and Xi Jinping in the national interest of the United States?,” former US ambassador to China Nicholas Burns asked on CNN’s “AC360” Tuesday. “Think of the symbolism. President Trump is throwing a lifeline to Vladimir Putin, who has been spurned for nearly five years because of his aggression in Ukraine.”
Burns, a veteran US diplomat, added: “He lavishes praise on Xi Jinping, which I think is directly contrary to what he should be saying about Xi Jinping, who’s an adversary of the United States.”
In every metric apart from the size of its nuclear arsenal, a remnant of the Soviet Union, Russia is an inferior power to the United States and China. But Trump often seems to elevate Putin, for instance with the recent sanctions-busting deal to buy Russian diesel or his invitation to Putin for the G20 summit at his Miami golf resort in December.
But Trump, like Putin, is looking for personal validation in Shenzhen. After his stunning rebuke from voters in the midterm elections, he needs to show the world, and Americans back home, that he’s no mere lame duck.
As host, Xi can lay on a show for China’s state media, posing as the dominant partner convening leaders of two other great powers.
The dangers of the summit are obvious, as nations such as Ukraine and those in Europe and in the Middle East wonder whether Xi, Trump and Putin will forge understandings that favor their own interests.
But there may be a case for the world’s most prominent nuclear powers to have open channels and regular meetings.
The world is hardly stable. And each leader has a stake in dangerous regional disputes — in Ukraine, Iran and Taiwan — that could spark global conflagration. A productive summit might defuse such flashpoints or even a nuclear arms race in space.
Criticism leveled at Trump that an offer of meetings is a concession is at times overblown. Talking to your enemies can be a sign of strength. In an inaugural address delivered amid soaring US-Soviet tensions, President John F. Kennedy said, “Civility is not a sign of weakness, and sincerity is always subject to proof. Let us never negotiate out of fear. But let us never fear to negotiate.”
Trump, Putin and Xi met late Wednesday at a welcome banquet for the APEC summit on the eve of their trilateral meeting. Retired US Navy Adm. James Stavridis told CNN’s Kasie Hunt that their encounter was a positive development.
“We’re not in ‘missiles flying.’ We’re not in a war with China,” said Stavridis, a former NATO supreme allied commander who is now a CNN military analyst. “There appears to me to be real warmth between President Xi and President Trump. I feel as though President Putin is … you can see it in these pictures, almost the odd man out here, which is where he ought to be.”
Trump is not the first modern president to open channels with US enemies. President Barack Obama acted on a pledge to do so that was criticized by his 2008 primary foe Hillary Clinton, making deals with Iran and Cuba. Trump reversed both openings with his hard-line policies.
Lyle Goldstein, director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities, a think tank that advocates a more restrained US global posture, recognizes the critique that Trump’s summits create good visuals and little else. But he believes that they can be useful nevertheless.
“I’m in favor of summits and meetings and engagement,” said Goldstein, who also leads the China Initiative at Brown University. Relations between Trump and Xi seems genuinely cordial, he added. “Let’s face it. Personal chemistry does matter, and Trump and Xi seem to be building a kind of chemistry.”
Such a connection could be critical to avoiding wider conflict in the event of a sudden crisis — perhaps over a naval confrontation in the South China Sea.
Trump has said that he also hopes to meet Kim in China. There’s an argument that his friendship with the brutal tyrant eased tensions during his first term. But their meetings failed to reverse North Korea’s nuclear program, and the Stalinist state now has more weapons and missiles than ever.
Goldstein also argued that the three-way summit format might become a more useful concept if it is repeated in future years because it could establish a framework for more regular progress.
Trump and Xi meet at a moment of extraordinary intrigue in US-China relations. The president has shrugged off reports that the former CEO of Nvidia had an affair with an executive flagged by US intelligence as a possible Chinese asset. The drama underscores China’s attempts to infiltrate US tech as the rivals’ AI race, which has huge military implications, heats up.
Trump’s first term Vice President Mike Pence told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins on Tuesday that the president should take a firm stance. “I’ve seen firsthand the rapport that he has with President Xi. I think he has the ability to speak forthrightly with him, and tell him what’s not acceptable to the United States of America and the things for which there will be consequences,” he said.
There’s another angle in Shenzhen that Trump may prefer not to think about. Barring revolutions, illness or death, Xi and Putin can expect to rule for years. Trump has the inconvenience of living in a democracy — one that has just delivered the kind of censure from which his authoritarian pals are immune.
That imbalance could have policy consequences. China may opt to stick to its characteristic long game in anticipation of yet another US policy reset with a new president in 2029. Putin may reason that he might score a better deal on Ukraine with Trump in office than with any other US president.
As summit host, Xi will seek to exploit Trump’s political frailties.
“The Chinese do see that Donald Trump is significantly weakened, first by the results of the midterm elections and then by the mishaps over the technological issues that happened in the last few days,” Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute

articles.title_orig: Prince Harry, after Ukraine trip, warns on threat from Russia
articles.title_zh: Prince Harry, after Ukraine trip, warns on threat from Russia
articles.content_orig:
The Duke of Sussex, who carried out a surprise visit to Ukraine at the weekend , has said he would rejoin the military if asked, as he warned of the threat from Russia.
He told the Telegraph he thought people were right to be nervous in the current international political climate and said it was time to "double our support" for Ukraine.
There appeared to be warnings about President Trump - with Prince Harry saying there was a big separation between what the American public thinks about Ukraine and the administration's attitude.
Prince Harry, able to speak more freely than working royals, said he hoped after the US mid-term elections it would be "fantastic to have more American support" for Ukraine.
Speaking to the Telegraph's Dominic Nicholls, Prince Harry said he thought the threat to Europe had been there for the past 15 years - and he felt like it had been at war for the past decade.
"Just because there's not drones, bullets, and rockets flying at us, it doesn't mean that we're not at war," said Prince Harry.
Prince Harry had been in Lviv in Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday - and had told the BBC and journalists at events that he thought the "rest of the world will continue to support" Ukraine.
He had told his Ukrainian hosts, about a conflict with Russia that has already lasted more than four years: "You're going to win the war."
In his Telegraph podcast, he called for a similar unity that was being shown by Ukraine, and feared that Europe could be divided and could "turn on itself".
He addressed the shifting position of US President Trump in a way that is unusual for a royal.
"I think there's been a big separation between what American society feels regarding support for Ukraine, which I think is incredibly high and always has been, compared to a certain group, or in, in this case, an administration that was perhaps thinking about it differently," said Prince Harry.
"As of January, things are going to change, so I think we should all be looking forward to that," he said, referring to the US mid-term elections, which saw significant setbacks for President Trump.
The BBC has approached the White House for comment.
Having served in the military in Afghanistan, Harry said he would return if needed for a future conflict: "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel."
Prince Harry had received an enthusiastic welcome when he visited Lviv in Ukraine at the weekend, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.
There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women, some of the 150,000 seriously wounded war veterans in the country.
His visit had been carried out with a press blackout for security reasons - and the night before journalists arrived in the city to cover the visit, there had been air raid warnings that had forced Prince Harry's planning team to head for the shelters.
"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," Prince Harry had said, including inventing new ways of treating the growing number of injured casualties.
"War is a terrible thing," he said in Lviv, but hailed the resilience of the Ukrainians who had been badly wounded in their defence against Russia's invasion.

articles.title_orig: Michigan Industry Leader Warns of Risks as Canada, China Discuss Auto Trade
articles.title_zh: Michigan Industry Leader Warns of Risks as Canada, China Discuss Auto Trade
articles.content_orig:
U.S.-China commission leaders warn of growing Chinese military capabilities, threats to Taiwan and risks to American security ahead of Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin.
President Donald Trump faces a potentially dangerous "two versus one" negotiating scenario when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, two senior members of a congressional China watchdog warned Wednesday, raising concerns that Beijing could seek concessions on Taiwan while Moscow pushes for greater U.S. pressure on Ukraine.
"I think it is two versus one. We have China and China's junior partner, Russia," Randall Schriver, chairman of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told Fox News Digital in a Zoom interview. "Largely they come to the table as a team versus President Trump and the United States," he said, citing China's support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as President Xi Jinping watches, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)
The warning comes ahead of Thursday's planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China , on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The high-stakes talks are expected to address issues such as the wars in Ukraine and Iran, trade and nuclear weapons.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, echoed Schriver's assessment, arguing that Moscow's growing dependence on Beijing puts Trump at a disadvantage.
"Putin is a client state of Xi Jinping, and that essentially means that President Trump is in the room with a two against one scenario, and the stakes are significant," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
"China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine, and they are basically the lifeblood of the Russian economy at this point," he added.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA
Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)
The commissioners spoke as the bipartisan body released its 2026 annual report to Congress , detailing Beijing's expanding military, technological and economic capabilities and the growing challenges they pose to American national security.
Asked what would constitute success or failure at the summit, Kuiken suggested Beijing would not have agreed to the meeting without assurances that its interests would be protected.
"My assessment is that the Chinese would never have agreed to this meeting if they had not had significant assurances that essentially nothing would happen," Kuiken said.
Schriver warned that both Xi and Putin would seek opportunities to advance their strategic objectives. He suggested Beijing would pursue gains related to Taiwan, while Moscow would hope Trump emerged from the meeting prepared to increase pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"If Putin had his way, Trump would emerge from the meeting and put more pressure on Zelenskyy," Schriver said.
He also questioned whether sufficient diplomatic groundwork had been laid for meaningful nuclear arms control discussions, one of the issues Trump has indicated he wants to address.
"President Trump would like to talk about nuclear disarmament, probably an agenda that makes sense. I'm just not sure we've done the front-end work when it comes to interagency work, bilateral or trilateral work, at a lower level to have a productive discussion there," Schriver said.
Nevertheless, Schriver suggested that avoiding concessions could itself represent a successful outcome for Washington.
"I think holding ground and just a restatement of U.S. interests is probably a victory of sorts for us," he said.
CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fabrication plant in Phoenix, Arizona, on March 3, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Beyond the summit, the commissioners warned that the United States faces mounting challenges as China approaches 2027, the benchmark year associated with Xi's directive for the People's Liberation Army to develop the capability to conduct a Taiwan military operation.
Asked whether Washington was doing enough to deter Chinese military action against the self-governing island, Schriver gave a blunt assessment.
"I think the short answer is no, we're not doing enough," he said.
Schriver pointed to a pause in congressional notifications for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan , saying the commission wants those notifications to proceed and supports stronger security assistance for the island.
He also warned that Beijing's increasingly sophisticated coercion tactics extend beyond conventional military operations to include actions involving its coast guard.
"We do talk about counter coercion capabilities and blending not only military capabilities but law enforcement that the Chinese are doing, this sort of blended lawfare with their coast guard east of Taiwan," Schriver said.
Taiwanese conscripts during a visit by Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te to a military base in Taichung on June 28, 2024. (Sam YehAFP via Getty Images)
"It's a tough challenge as we're entering the benchmark year that Xi Jinping said of 2027. There should be more attention to this and there should be greater efforts to this."
Kuiken emphasized Taiwan's importance to the global technology supply chain, particularly its role in manufacturing advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence.
"Taiwan is the island at the center of the world. Xi Jinping is obsessed with it," he said.
Pointing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, Kuiken warned of the broader implications for American technological leadership if Beijing were to take military action against the island.
He urged Washington and its partners to develop a coordinated strategy to make an invasion or other Chinese coercive measures against Taiwan unattractive to Beijing.
President Donald Trump meets with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel, on Nov. 17, 2026, in Manila, Philippines. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Responding to concerns about Taiwan , a U.S. official told Fox News Digital, "There is no change to our policy with respect to Taiwan." Asked about the commissioners’ warnings, a White House official emphasized President Trump’s diplomatic approach to China and his plans to discuss nuclear arms reduction during the trilateral summit.
"Under President Trump’s leadership, U.S.-China relations have been refocused on what matters most – rebuilding the safety, security and prosperity of Americans. And as President Trump has said: much has been, and will be, accomplished, between the two leaders," the official said.
"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the President of the United States, the President of the People’s Republic of China, and the President of the Russian Federation."
"The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," the official added.
TRUMP’S TAIWAN ‘NEGOTIATING CHIP’ REMARK SPARKS ALARM OVER HOW FAR HE'D SHIFT US-CHINA POLICY

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Gulf states and tankers under fire as U.S. and Iran ramp back up tit-for-tat strikes
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Gulf states and tankers under fire as U.S. and Iran ramp back up tit-for-tat strikes
articles.content_orig:
An unknown projectile struck a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, according to the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations .
The maritime agency said local authorities reported that the incident took place north of Khasab, Oman. The projectile hit the engine room while the vessel was transiting outbound through the strait.
"The crew are safe and accounted for. Damage assessment, and environmental impact are unknown at the time of this report," the UKMTO said.
The USS George Washington has left the Middle East and is now in the 7th Fleet, the Navy's numbered fleet for the Indo-Pacific, a Navy official confirmed to CBS News on Wednesday.
That brings the number of aircraft carriers in the Middle East back down to two — the USS George H.W. Bush and the newly arrived USS Theodore Roosevelt .
The USS George Washington is homeported at Yosuka, Japan, and may be headed back there along with the escort destroyers in the George Washington carrier strike group. The aircraft carrier, with its approximately 5,000 personnel, entered the Middle East in August to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln amid reports of low morale and food shortages aboard that carrier.
Yemen's Houthi militants on Wednesday targeted Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport and a financial center in Riyadh, Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on social media .
Saree said "a large number of cruise missiles" achieved "precise and direct hits" on targets in Saudi Arabia's capital.
"This attack comes in response to the Saudi enemy's targeting of civilian infrastructure in our beloved country," he said.
The U.S. is warning Americans in Bahrain to be extra careful after at least four attempted strikes by Iran in the last week.
"Americans in Bahrain should exercise heightened vigilance due to the increased threat of armed attacks by Iranian-supported Houthis and Iranian efforts to target U.S. government officials and facilities in the region," the U.S. Embassy said in a new security alert issued Wednesday. "Be aware of potential alerts, flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions."
All of the launches were intercepted before causing any harm, according to U.S. Central Command. Iran was reportedly targeting U.S. radar sites in Bahrain. The latest round on Wednesday included attacks directed at Kuwait as well.
CENTCOM put out a statement on Wednesday afternoon saying no American military personnel have been injured in any of the strikes launched this week in a rebuttal to apparent rumors spreading online, it said.
The U.S. Treasury has targeted funding for the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group in its latest round of sanctions tied to Operation Economic Outcast.
One of the targets of the sanctions was the Wa Ta'awanu Association, which the U.S. said is a charity that "provides cover for Hizballah's activities under the guise of delivering humanitarian services."
"The Iranian regime's attempts to infringe on Lebanon's sovereignty through terror proxies like Hizballah will not be tolerated," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "The U.S. government will continue to disrupt Iran's attempts to exert influence in the region and fund its proxies."
The sanctions also targeted an alleged gold and cash smuggling network run by Hezbollah and the IRGC's Quds Force.
The Hezbollah militant group has been fighting Israel in southern Lebanon for years, but the latest round of violence was sparked in the wake of the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran in February. In solidarity, Hezbollah began targeting northern Israel with missile and drone launches, prompting an invasion by Israel.
The chief of Israel's military, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, met with U.S. Central Command leader Adm. Brad Cooper in Tel Aviv on Wednesday to discuss the current situation in the Middle East.
"During the meeting, the participants discussed regional developments and shared security challenges," Israeli officials said in a statement. "They also addressed the importance of deepening strategic and operational cooperation between the two militaries, strengthening coordination, and enhancing joint readiness to address a range of scenarios."
CENTCOM oversees military action in the Middle East and Cooper has become an important member of the Trump administration's Defense Department.
In addition, Zamir, Cooper and Mossad Director Roman Gofman took part in a trilateral meeting. Mossad is Israel's foreign intelligence agency, similar to the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency.
The U.S. and Israel have been debating whether to restart larger military action against Iran in the past several weeks after talks prior to Election Day fell apart. The U.S. launched a strike on Qeshm Island on Tuesday, which was categorized as self-defense after Iran had launched unsuccessful strikes against Bahrain multiple times this week.
A powerful explosion rattled homes in Riyadh on Wednesday, AFP journalists and residents said, as Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis pressed their campaign of attacks against Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis also said they intercepted two cruise missiles — the latest in weeks of strikes targeting military, civilian and oil infrastructure.
Later on Wednesday, the coalition said it had intercepted two drones launched by the Houthis in the Riyadh and southern regions, after Saudi authorities had issued and later lifted an alert for the southern Sharurah governorate.
Residents said Wednesday's explosion came without warning, with no cellphone alert issued beforehand as is usually the case during aerial threats.
"The explosion was extremely loud," said a resident in northern Riyadh. "Hearing a blast without receiving a warning is very frightening."
An AFP journalist said doors throughout her home swung open and the lights briefly went out.
The location of the explosion was not immediately clear, but residents told AFP they saw smoke near Riyadh's airport in the northeast of the city.
U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Wednesday that Iranian threats inside and outside the U.S. have "dramatically increased."
"We remain committed to detecting, deterring and combatting the Iranian lethal plotting outside the United States and inside the United States," Clayton told members of the House Homeland Security Committee during a hearing. "These threats have dramatically increased."
He emphasized the danger posed by online radicalization, describing how foreign extremist networks can influence individuals already living inside the United States.
"That's not theoretical; it's real," Clayton said.
Deputy FBI Director Christopher Raia noted that intelligence about possible plots does not necessarily mean would-be attackers have the capability to carry out the plans.
"A lot of the reporting is largely aspirational," Raia said. "But that does not mean we do not take it seriously."
Saudi Arabia is preparing for its war against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen to last well into 2027, the Reuters news agency reported Wednesday, citing two Western officials briefed by the kingdom about its planning.
Fighting in Yemen's grueling civil war between the Houthi rebels and Yemen's Saudi-backed government had largely stopped after a ceasefire was signed in 2022, but reignited over the summer as the war launched by the U.S. and Israel against Iran sent tension across the Middle East surging.
The exchange of fire between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been more intense than the other fronts in the intertwined Middle Eastern conflicts since U.S.-Iran hostilities eased late in the summer. Thousands of people have been killed and hundreds of thousands displaced in Yemen, and Houthi rockets have killed at least 20 people in Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_orig: PlayStation suffers widespread network problems hours before release of GTA VI
articles.title_zh: PlayStation suffers widespread network problems hours before release of GTA VI
articles.content_orig:
Disruption comes at critical moment, with Grand Theft Auto VI one of the most eagerly anticipated titles in history
PlayStation has suffered widespread network problems just hours before the release of Grand Theft Auto VI , one of the most eagerly anticipated titles in recent gaming history.
The disruption emerged Wednesday, causing frustrated players to flood social media with complaints about failed logins and server connection problems downloading games and updates.
PlayStation’s official network status page acknowledged problems affecting its gaming and social services, which has left players struggling to access online features.
“You might have difficulty launching games, apps, or network features. We’re working to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Thank you for your patience,” the alert read.
Many affected users said their internet connections were working normally, suggesting the problems were specifically affecting PlayStation’s online services. Some PS5 owners said that their consoles successfully completed internet connection tests, only for the “Sign in to online services” check to fail.
The scale of the disruption was reflected on Downdetector , a website that tracks real-time service outages, which cited 1,228 user reports of PlayStation outages by Wednesday afternoon.
The website monitors disruptions using reports submitted by users, with sudden spikes potentially indicating that large numbers of people are experiencing similar technical difficulties. The reports do not independently confirm the extent of an official outage, however.
Although no official cause has been established, the timing of the problems has raised questions about whether the issue could be linked to a recently released PS5 software update. Sony announced Tuesday evening that it had rolled out a system software update required for users planning to play GTA VI.
Sony’s official troubleshooting advice recommends that affected players examine their system software and internet connections.
The disruption comes at a critical moment for PlayStation users, with GTA VI scheduled to launch at midnight Thursday.
GTA VI is being lauded as the most anticipated game in history. The hype for the latest installment of the iconic GTA franchise, the first new game in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has already suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game.

articles.title_orig: Fed Saw Need to Keep Raising Rates Despite Holding Steady in October
articles.title_zh: Fed Saw Need to Keep Raising Rates Despite Holding Steady in October
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Federal Reserve governor Chris Waller said Wednesday that if the central bank hikes interest rates by a quarter point next month, it will need to signal that the Fed will hike again by that much in January.
Otherwise, the Fed needs to raise rates by a jumbo half percentage point in December.
"People have argued, do you do 50 in December, nothing in January, or 25 in December, 25 in January," Waller said in an interview Wednesday on CNBC. "But when you do 25 now and you're going to do 25 in January, it only affects market pricing if you signal you're going to do it, and you give the markets a credible signal."
Waller said that if you leave the market guessing about a January rate increase, there won't be an effect on the market and, by extension, the economy.
"If you're not going to signal this very clearly to markets you're going in January, my view is then you have to go 50 in December," Waller said.
Read more: How the Fed rate decision affects your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments
That sounds a lot like forward guidance, which Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has sought to eliminate since taking the reins in May. Warsh has said that telegraphing future policy moves distorts market signals and boxes in policymakers.
But Warsh's philosophy hasn't quite taken hold, as other Fed members have continued to offer clues about the path ahead — which has also led to more questions and at times confusion in markets.
Without using the term explicitly, Waller argued Wednesday that the Fed would need to use forward guidance if it doesn't deliver a jumbo hike next month. He said the central bank could signal its next move either in the statement or at Warsh's press conference. He added that quarterly interest rate projections, which will be released in December, would be helpful this time because it's the end of the year and the projections would be for all of next year.
Waller said the Fed needs to be more aggressive because inflation is moving higher after remaining above the central bank's 2% goal for nearly six years.
Read more: How to protect your savings against inflation
Waller first hinted at a jumbo hike last week, saying ahead of the Consumer Price Index release, that if inflation came in higher than expected, stronger action would be needed.
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October, compared with expectations of 0.3%. "Core" inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3%, compared with expectations of 0.2%.
On Wednesday, Waller said the Fed needs to take back the three rate cuts from last year and may need to do more to get inflation to come back down.
New York Federal Reserve president John Williams doesn't share that view.
Asked Tuesday during a Q&A with Axios in New York whether that latest inflation data calls for a supersize rate hike soon, Williams said, "I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action."

articles.title_orig: China watchdog warns Trump faces ‘2-on-1’ showdown with Xi, Putin as Taiwan risks mount
articles.title_zh: China watchdog warns Trump faces ‘2-on-1’ showdown with Xi, Putin as Taiwan risks mount
articles.content_orig:
U.S.-China commission leaders warn of growing Chinese military capabilities, threats to Taiwan and risks to American security ahead of Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin.
President Donald Trump faces a potentially dangerous "two versus one" negotiating scenario when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, two senior members of a congressional China watchdog warned Wednesday, raising concerns that Beijing could seek concessions on Taiwan while Moscow pushes for greater U.S. pressure on Ukraine.
"I think it is two versus one. We have China and China's junior partner, Russia," Randall Schriver, chairman of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told Fox News Digital in a Zoom interview. "Largely they come to the table as a team versus President Trump and the United States," he said, citing China's support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as President Xi Jinping watches, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)
The warning comes ahead of Thursday's planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China , on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The high-stakes talks are expected to address issues such as the wars in Ukraine and Iran, trade and nuclear weapons.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, echoed Schriver's assessment, arguing that Moscow's growing dependence on Beijing puts Trump at a disadvantage.
"Putin is a client state of Xi Jinping, and that essentially means that President Trump is in the room with a two against one scenario, and the stakes are significant," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
"China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine, and they are basically the lifeblood of the Russian economy at this point," he added.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA
Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)
The commissioners spoke as the bipartisan body released its 2026 annual report to Congress , detailing Beijing's expanding military, technological and economic capabilities and the growing challenges they pose to American national security.
Asked what would constitute success or failure at the summit, Kuiken suggested Beijing would not have agreed to the meeting without assurances that its interests would be protected.
"My assessment is that the Chinese would never have agreed to this meeting if they had not had significant assurances that essentially nothing would happen," Kuiken said.
Schriver warned that both Xi and Putin would seek opportunities to advance their strategic objectives. He suggested Beijing would pursue gains related to Taiwan, while Moscow would hope Trump emerged from the meeting prepared to increase pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"If Putin had his way, Trump would emerge from the meeting and put more pressure on Zelenskyy," Schriver said.
He also questioned whether sufficient diplomatic groundwork had been laid for meaningful nuclear arms control discussions, one of the issues Trump has indicated he wants to address.
"President Trump would like to talk about nuclear disarmament, probably an agenda that makes sense. I'm just not sure we've done the front-end work when it comes to interagency work, bilateral or trilateral work, at a lower level to have a productive discussion there," Schriver said.
Nevertheless, Schriver suggested that avoiding concessions could itself represent a successful outcome for Washington.
"I think holding ground and just a restatement of U.S. interests is probably a victory of sorts for us," he said.
CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fabrication plant in Phoenix, Arizona, on March 3, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Beyond the summit, the commissioners warned that the United States faces mounting challenges as China approaches 2027, the benchmark year associated with Xi's directive for the People's Liberation Army to develop the capability to conduct a Taiwan military operation.
Asked whether Washington was doing enough to deter Chinese military action against the self-governing island, Schriver gave a blunt assessment.
"I think the short answer is no, we're not doing enough," he said.
Schriver pointed to a pause in congressional notifications for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan , saying the commission wants those notifications to proceed and supports stronger security assistance for the island.
He also warned that Beijing's increasingly sophisticated coercion tactics extend beyond conventional military operations to include actions involving its coast guard.
"We do talk about counter coercion capabilities and blending not only military capabilities but law enforcement that the Chinese are doing, this sort of blended lawfare with their coast guard east of Taiwan," Schriver said.
Taiwanese conscripts during a visit by Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te to a military base in Taichung on June 28, 2024. (Sam YehAFP via Getty Images)
"It's a tough challenge as we're entering the benchmark year that Xi Jinping said of 2027. There should be more attention to this and there should be greater efforts to this."
Kuiken emphasized Taiwan's importance to the global technology supply chain, particularly its role in manufacturing advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence.
"Taiwan is the island at the center of the world. Xi Jinping is obsessed with it," he said.
Pointing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, Kuiken warned of the broader implications for American technological leadership if Beijing were to take military action against the island.
He urged Washington and its partners to develop a coordinated strategy to make an invasion or other Chinese coercive measures against Taiwan unattractive to Beijing.
President Donald Trump meets with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel, on Nov. 17, 2026, in Manila, Philippines. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Responding to concerns about Taiwan , a U.S. official told Fox News Digital, "There is no change to our policy with respect to Taiwan." Asked about the commissioners’ warnings, a White House official emphasized President Trump’s diplomatic approach to China and his plans to discuss nuclear arms reduction during the trilateral summit.
"Under President Trump’s leadership, U.S.-China relations have been refocused on what matters most – rebuilding the safety, security and prosperity of Americans. And as President Trump has said: much has been, and will be, accomplished, between the two leaders," the official said.
"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the President of the United States, the President of the People’s Republic of China, and the President of the Russian Federation."
"The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," the official added.
TRUMP’S TAIWAN ‘NEGOTIATING CHIP’ REMARK SPARKS ALARM OVER HOW FAR HE'D SHIFT US-CHINA POLICY
A procession of Taiwanese armed military vehicles patrols outside the Songshan Airport in the capital city following China’s announcement of the military exercise Joint Sword-2024B that encircles Taiwan, Oct. 14, 2024, in Taipei, Taiwan. (Daniel

articles.title_orig: Trump and Xi are set to meet in China amid tensions over AI. Here's what to know.
articles.title_zh: Trump and Xi are set to meet in China amid tensions over AI. Here's what to know.
articles.content_orig:
Washington — President Trump is holding a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, against the backdrop of a widening scandal over advanced U.S. chips reaching China and internal divisions within Mr. Trump's Cabinet about how to address it.
The bilateral meeting is taking place in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, known as APEC. Mr. Trump embraced Xi when he arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday.
It's the third time the two world leaders are meeting face to face this year. The last time they met was in September, when Mr. Trump hosted Xi for a three-day summit at the White House. Mr. Trump is hosting Xi again for the G20 Leaders' Summit at Trump National Doral in Miami in December.
The Trump-Xi meeting will be followed by a meeting of Mr. Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Here's what Mr. Trump and Xi are likely to discuss.
Mr. Trump told reporters as he left for Asia that he may bring up Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The Justice Department has been investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed for diverting semiconductor chips to China.
The president has cast doubts on assessments that Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset.
"I don't know that she is a spy," he said. "Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country, that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."
Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the scandal is much bigger than Jensen Huang and his alleged affairs.
"It's really kind of unfolded into a much bigger, longer-term scandal that involves the question of how many chips did China get, how porous were export controls, and how did the Commerce Department enforce them?" McGuire said on a phone briefing with reporters Wednesday. "Which I think is a much more important, longer-term strategic question for the United States, for the U.S.-China relationship than anything involving Jensen Huang's personal affairs."
Shortly before the president left for Asia, the Trump administration announced new interim trade rules that will restrict Chinese AI companies from accessing advanced U.S. chips remotely.
The move comes after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of slow-walking restrictions on Megaspeed, revealing a rift between Bessent and Lutnick. Bessent told CNBC that Mr. Trump had indicated that China should not have access to the chips, but suggested that Lutnick was resisting. The president didn't take sides in the Bessent-Lutnick debate, telling reporters before he left for Asia that the men have "two different views" where "one wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China."
"One view is you don't want to insult China," Mr. Trump said Monday. "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them. And the other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do. Both can say either is wrong or right."
Ultimately, the Treasury Department and National Security Council, not the Commerce Department under Lutnick, wrote  the new interim rule cutting off Chinese companies from remotely accessing the most advanced AI chips in data centers abroad, though the Commerce Department issued the rule.
"This is a very significant action that really cuts off a lot of the avenues that China is using to get AI computing power," McGuire said. "There was a digital forensic study that was done recently that showed that every single advanced Chinese model is actually trained with the most advanced American chips, so even though these chips have been banned to China, the controls have not been effective. They've probably had some impact but not that much."
The actions taken on Monday, however, will have a "really significant" effect on China's access to computing power, which "could materially widen the lead" between the U.S. and China on AI, McGuire said.
Mr. Trump has shown no signs of wanting to slow the United States' AI advancement in the race against China. After a September summit between Mr. Trump and Xi, the U.S. and Chinese governments pledged to set up a communication channel to share information when AI goes off the rails.
But talking about wayward AI incidents after the fact isn't nearly enough, said Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow on technology with the Asia Society Policy Institute and a digital fellow with the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI.
Graylin will be interested to see if Mr. Trump and Xi can work past the negative news cycle, like the Jensen Huang scandal, to take more steps on AI safety collaboration by bringing together more technical experts for working-level discussions.
"I hope that we go beyond just having surface level discussion, and we start to actually create some enduring institutions around safety," Graylin said.
Before leaving for Asia, Mr. Trump was asked if he'll bring up Taiwan in his meeting with Xi.
"I'm sure he'll raise it," the president responded. "I won't have to raise it."
David Sacks, a senior fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations — not the former White House AI czar David Sacks — said he thinks that's right.
"I think that it's very clear that every time Xi sees Trump, they do a little check-in on Taiwan, and Xi Jinping raises his concerns on Taiwan and his expectations of how President Trump will handle Taiwan and cross-strait dynamics," Sacks told reporters on the Council on Foreign Relations call.
A $14 billion arms package to Taiwan is still pending on the president's desk, Sacks said. Earlier this year, the Navy said the arms sale had been put on "pause" to make sure the U.S. military had enough munitions for the Iran war. Sacks said there will be "more pressure from Congress in the coming months to move that arms package forward."
"And so, if President Trump is determined to resist that, you know he will need, you know — Xi Jinping will hope to kind of stiffen his spine and say, 'You're on the right track, and if you approve this arms package, you're going to send cross-strait relations reeling.'"
Lyle Goldstein, the director of Defense Priorities Asia, told CBS News he is actually optimistic about a Trump-Putin-Xi meeting. Goldstein said he doesn't think any "major results" will come out of the sit-down, but the discussions might bear fruit in a future U.S.-China-Russia meeting.
"I actually think it could allow for some, not for breakthroughs, but for some movement on major issues," Goldstein said. "And this is the first time ever that you have this trilateral format for Russia, China, and the U.S. So I would like to see this continue."
Mr. Trump said he has a range of topics to discuss with both Xi and Putin when they meet, including denuclearization.
"We're going to talk about denuclearization," Mr. Trump said. "Tough subject, because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right? Especially since you do have other countries."
They'll also discuss Iran, the U.S. president said. On Tuesday, Mr. Trump said Iran would have a major price to pay if it detonates a so-called dirty bomb, after CNN reported U.S. intelligence indicates Iran may be developing plans to set off such a device in the nation's capital.
The White House previously said Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion in the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting, since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said Ukraine will be a topic for the three leaders.
"We'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine," he told reporters.
