articles.title_orig: Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.title_zh: Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.content_orig:
Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.
Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.
It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.
Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second to the north in Gaza City, and the third in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".
At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title_orig: Britain, EU drop 'trusted partnership' term from summit draft
articles.title_zh: Britain, EU drop 'trusted partnership' term from summit draft
articles.content_orig:
Leaked text of 72-paragraph second draft shows agreement has largely been reached before expected signoff on Friday
The UK-EU “relationship reset” agreement, which began in earnest under Keir Starmer, is expected to be signed off by Andy Burnham in Brussels on Friday.
A leaked text of the second draft shows an agreement has largely been reached with some outstanding points.
Here’s what is and isn’t addressed in the 72-paragraph joint communique, from pet passports and cheese imports to student fees and artist touring visas.
You may not make it. The deal states it will “allow people from the EU and the UK to reside for up to three years to engage in activities such as work, studies, au pairing, volunteering, or simply travelling”.
But the deal may not be active until 2030 because work permits are the preserve of national governments, not something Brussels can solve.
“We aim to apply this agreement no later than 2028 and endeavour to ensure that opportunities under the scheme will be available to our young people no later than January 2030,” the draft says.
This has yet to be agreed. The two options in the draft text are a halfway house between international and home fees, or a concession from the UK to allow EU citizens pay the same as British students (or Irish ones, who are also eligible for home fees under a separate longstanding agreement).
The choices, according to the draft, are “significantly reduced undergraduate” or “equal treatment” with UK nationals on tuition fees.
The British government wants to cap youth mobility at between 50,000 and 80,000 places to reduce impact on overall migration numbers. The EU is pushing for at least 100,000.
Some EU states, including Germany, are open to the idea of allowing unlimited numbers of British young people to work, live or study in their countries regardless of UK reciprocation.
Elton John has long been among those demanding the government fix a flaw in the Brexit deal which saw gigging bands or theatre groups unable to tour Europe without major bureaucracy (and its associated cost) since 2021.
The EU has resisted negotiating on the issue because, like youth mobility, it touches on work permits which are a national remit. But in what appears to be a win for the UK, touring artists do feature in the draft text.
No deal been reached, but it has been agreed that “the EU and the UK should explore further mutually beneficial solutions” for “touring artists”.
Not yet. The draft agreement says the sanitary and phyto-sanitary (SPS) agreement will not be implemented until 1 March 2028.
This takes into account primary legislation that is needed on the UK side to dynamically align with EU standards.
No. These are tied to the SPS deal, meaning British travellers will still have to fork out up to £200 every time they take their dog or cat to an EU country.
Travel and transport officials are hoping relevant changes to the SPS agreement can be brought forward.
“Around 15% of our customers have pets with them. For them it will make a huge difference,” Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the owner of Eurotunnel, told the Guardian.
No. The EU has pressed the UK to follow its trade defence measures which include quotas on Chinese hybrid-electric cars and tariffs on fully electric cars.
The UK has said it will not be coerced into a decision but is demanding that British manufacturers are not locked out of the upcoming Made in Europe legislation in exchange for forming a kind of trade club with the EU on autos.
Both sides agree to protectionist measures in “a particular supply chain” but there is no agreement yet on how that will apply. According to the text, the EU proposes that “the UK would be bound to ensure in its policies and national legal order the same outcomes” as measures imposed by the EU. The UK’s proposed text says: “We will aim to protect supply chains consistently across our markets and guard against potential risks of circumvention.”
It’s gone. Instead of a vague “trusted partnership”, both sides commit to a “partnership for economic resilience”.
The language in the latest draft agreement has also been tightened up in a concession to the UK, say diplomats.
The UK wants to restore pre-Brexit access to EU databases but this will not be agreed on Friday. The EU will instead explore giving the UK access to its proposed Prüm International scheme “on data exchange for police cooperation to chosen third-country partners”.
There is no mention of Eurodac, the database that stores biometrics of asylum seekers in the EU, and diplomats say sharing this data, which was not collected for law enforcement purposes, could be tricky.
But according to the draft, the EU will “continue exploring ways to reinforce mutual and reciprocal exchanges of data on criminal records of third-country nationals”.

articles.title_zh: New leaks detail next year’s iPhone Pro redesign and iPhone Duo 2
articles.content_orig:
Next year’s fall iPhone lineup is expected to include 20th anniversary redesigned Pro models and an iPhone Duo 2. Here’s what to expect per the latest leaks.
Rumors for next year’s flagship new iPhone models are ramping up. Earlier today, we got a release timing update on iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 and learned that Apple may have multiple iPhone 20 Pro designs in testing.
Now more details have arrived via Weibo leakers Digital Chat Station and Fixed Focus Digital, who focus on the highly-anticipated new iPhone Pro models and also the iPhone Duo 2.
Fixed Focus Digital says the ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ will indeed return to a curved design, similar to the iPhone Air with more rounded edges. This echoes what the leaker shared earlier this week , but there’s one new tidbit: he says early prototypes include a titanium frame.
Apple used titanium for the iPhone 15 Pro and 16 Pro, then abandoned it with the 17 Pro and 18 Pro. Titanium is used on the iPhone Air though. With next year’s 20th anniversary Pro models taking design cues from the Air, it sounds like titanium could return.
Leaker Digital Chat Station, in a reply to this post about iPhone Duo 2, adds that the 20 Pro series will be larger in size and have a bezel-free, quad-curved display.
Regarding the Duo 2, he says it will have the same 7.6-inch inner display and 5.4-inch outer display as the first model. The side button with integrated Touch ID remains unchanged as well.
On the possibility of Face ID being added, he says it’s “questionable.” He suggests internal components might require too many changes, but doesn’t offer inside information.
Which new model are you more interested in: the iPhone 20 Pro or iPhone Duo 2? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: Fed Officials Saw Higher Rates Ahead When They Held Steady Last Month
articles.title_zh: Fed Officials Saw Higher Rates Ahead When They Held Steady Last Month
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve officials expressed confidence in October that further interest rate increases will be needed to stem inflation, though they decided to hold off while gathering more information, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday.
Policymakers put artificial intelligence at the core of their discussions, indicating that demand associated with the technology would be "a material source of inflation risk."
More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple of participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December.
The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective."
In a CNBC interview Wednesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller reiterated his belief that the Federal Open Market Committee should consider a half-point hike in December.
Officials at the meeting expressed a high level of concern over AI, both as a source of inflation and financial instability.
Fed staff members who briefed participants noted "that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint."
"Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures," the minutes said. "A few participants remarked that AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms."
Officials said they still expect inflation to fall off sharply in 2027 and beyond as the impact from the current shocks wear off.
Ultimately, the FOMC voted 10-2 to keep its benchmark overnight borrowing rate locked in a range between 3.75%-4%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase.
Those voting in favor of the hold "pointed to benefits in accumulating additional information, which would help in determining the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
Since the meeting, the inflation data has shown that the pace of price increases remains well above target.
The consumer price index in October rose 0.4% for all items and 0.3% for the core that excludes food and energy. Both readings were 0.1 percentage point higher than expected.
While indicating concern over how stubborn inflation has been, most Fed officials who have spoken publicly advocated a patient approach.
However, Waller said Wednesday that the Fed may have to "shock" markets by approving a half-point hike in December. He is the only central banker to espouse that belief publicly, though St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said he anticipates as much as a full percentage point move higher by the spring of 2027. As governor, Waller is a permanent FOMC voter; Musalem will not vote until 2028.
Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Friday on CNBC that the central bank risks losing its credibility if it doesn't act.
At the core of policymakers' concern is whether rising prices related to the Iran war and President Donald Trump 's tariffs, in many cases temporary events that wouldn't prompt a response, are instead becoming more entrenched.
Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting that includes low odds of a half-point move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Futures traders also are pricing a solid likelihood of two more increases in 2027.

articles.title_orig: Xreal Aura Review: Solid AR Glasses Hampered By Google's Half-Baked Android XR
articles.title_zh: Xreal Aura Review: Solid AR Glasses Hampered By Google's Half-Baked Android XR
articles.content_orig:
For $1,099, we should expect more.
Two years after Google announced Android XR , and a year after Samsung's flagship $1,800 Galaxy XR headset landed with a fizzle, Google's latest stab at mixed reality is finally starting to seem... real. We've taken a look at the first batch of Android XR smart glasses , which are landing this fall and take aim at Meta's popular Ray-Ban smart frames. Now Xreal is launching its Aura XR headset , which is the most intriguing Android XR device we've seen yet. It builds on Xreal's impressive history of virtual display glasses , adding just enough smarts to make it a viable, and far cheaper, alternative to Apple's Vision Pro. But with a starting price of $1,279 (on sale for $1,099 through December), it's still mainly targeted at VR developers.
Much like the baffling launch of Googlebooks, though, I'm not yet convinced that solid hardware will be able to save an ecosystem that Google isn't truly committed to. It's taken the company several years to actually deliver Android XR devices most people can actually afford, and there still aren't many notable apps that truly show off what the platform can do. Making Google Maps more immersive isn't enough.
Still, the Xreal Aura is a sign that Android XR hardware is more than just vaporware, and it's significantly cheaper than last year's Galaxy XR. It's also a glimpse of what we'll see with the upcoming Meta VR Glasses, and perhaps a sign of how Apple could actually follow up on the promise of the Vision Pro.
The Xreal Aura is essentially a souped-up version of the company's already excellent display glasses, except it's connected to a wired Compute Puck that houses all of the hardware necessary to run Android XR. The Aura's sunglasses-like frames look almost the same as the Xreal One Pro , except it also features cameras for spatial sensing, finger tracking and capturing photos and video. Xreal's transparent frames let you easily see the world around you, without the need for complicated camera pass-through functionality like the Galaxy XR and Apple Vision Pro use. You can also darken the screen to completely black out the world, similar to what you'd see on a typical VR headset.
Like Xreal's previous display glasses, the Aura relies on tiny micro-OLED screens with a resolution slightly beyond 1080p (1,920 by 1,200). They can reach up to 1,058 nits of brightness, which is slightly less than the 1,200 nits on the new Xreal One Pro+, and they support up to a 120Hz resolution with external devices. (The Android XR interface only runs at 72Hz.) The Aura's 70-degree field of view (FOV) is the best we've seen from Xreal, but it's also well below what we've seen on dedicated VR headsets, which use larger screens to completely fill your vision. The Apple Vision Pro reaches a FOV of around 100 degrees, while the Meta Quest 3 and many other headsets reach up to 110 degrees.
For processing power, the Compute Puck houses a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite system-on-a-chip, and either 12GB or 16GB of RAM (alongside either 256GB or 512GB of storage). It also features Xreal's custom X1S spatial processor, a slightly improved version of the X1 chip on earlier frames, and it looks similar to the Vision Pro's battery pack. It has two USB-C ports, one for connecting to the Aura's frames and the other for either charging or connecting to a separate device. The top portion of the Compute Puck also serves as a trackpad, which is helpful for navigating Android XR without holding your hand up.
When you plug in another device into the Compute Puck, its video output shows up in a single Android XR window, which you can resize at will (and also position alongside other Android XR apps). You can also plug the Aura's frames directly into computers and other devices, where it functions exactly like the company's previous display glasses. That could be useful when you just need a big virtual screen, and you don't want to deal with the hassle of juggling the Compute Puck.
The Xreal Aura is exceptionally comfortable to wear; the frames weigh just 95 grams (0.2 pounds) on their own, compared to the 1.6-pound Vision Pro. The Aura is also fantastic for watching movies on a gigantic virtual display and it's incredibly useful if you need a large virtual monitor. But it's also crystal clear that Android XR is still in its infancy, as there aren't many notable apps to show off the platform. Using Android XR also doesn't feel very different than using any other Android device — as if Google made very little effort to reshape its OS around mixed reality. (There are definitely shades of the same laziness that annoyed me with Googlebooks.)
It doesn't help that apps crash often in Android XR, or that its core hand recognition interface feels lackluster. The Xreal Aura is often slow to respond to where my finger is pointing, or recognize when I'm pinching my fingers to select something. That's annoying enough when simply navigating Chrome or YouTube, but it's infuriating when trying to play an XR game like Cubism , which relies on placing 3D blocks in very specific places. Pointing at everything just to navigate Android XR also gets tiring over time — there's no eye-tracking like on the Vision Pro, which makes selecting on-screen elements a cinch. I quickly grew to prefer navigating Android XR with the Compute Puck's trackpad instead of pointing at everything.
I was able to sit back and actually enjoy the Xreal Aura while watching the opening of Casino Royale on Prime Video, as well as a few episodes of the new Ghost in the Shell series. Xreal's micro-OLED displays deliver vibrant and colorful video, and its speakers built into the Aura's thick frames sound great. The Aura is also an excellent companion for laptops: I was able to have a giant screen mirroring my MacBook Air while playing the YouTube app right beside it.
Still, I wish there was more to actually do in Android XR. Zooming around the world in Google Maps' immersive view is fun, and I appreciated revisiting VR experiences like Cosmos Unseen: Black Holes, but they're not as enthralling as they are in traditional VR headsets. Being able to see the outside world easily is both a blessing and a curse on the Xreal Aura. You can also see spatial versions of pictures in the Google Photos app, which is cool at first, but quickly starts to feel gimmicky. Similarly, I didn't see much point to Android XR's Spatial Mode, which converts everything you see into pseudo-3D. It just gave me a headache while browsing the web.
Third-party support is clearly lackluster, especially when it comes to entertainment apps. All I saw was HBO Max and Prime Video, no Disney+ or Netflix (which isn't on visionOS, to be fair). You'll have to watch all of your other streaming services through Chrome, which isn't exactly a premium experience. It's also a particularly bad look when Meta just recently launched 3D movie support (including within the Disney+ app) on the Quest 3, 3S and its upcoming VR Glasses . That's something Google could eventually bring to Android XR, but who knows when that will happen.
Even the first-party YouTube app is a disappointment. There's a specific section for immersive videos, but it's filled with the same blurry 360-degree content we've been seeing for years. There's no big push for higher-resolution 180-degree 3D video like we've seen on the Vision Pro, or that Meta has announced for its VR Glasses.
Android XR is such a barren landscape, I sometimes found it more useful to just directly connect the Xreal Aura to my laptop or phone. At that point, it acts purely as a virtual display, but I found it helpful when I just wanted to stream a TV show in a crowded or tight space. The downside here is that connecting another device to the Compute Puck involves juggling a second USB-C cable, which can easily become frustrating. The Vision Pro can wirelessly connect to Macs, so it manages to avoid this issue.

articles.title_orig: Ford ships first battery cells using CATL technology
articles.title_zh: Ford ships first battery cells using CATL technology
articles.content_orig:
MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.
The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck , which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.
The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.
The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.
Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible.
"If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells."
The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.
Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.
Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.
Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.
The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

articles.title_orig: El Salvador’s president confirms and celebrates attack on home of key Haitian gang leader
articles.title_zh: El Salvador’s president confirms and celebrates attack on home of key Haitian gang leader
articles.content_orig:
Demonstrators have marched in several Haitian cities to show support for a deployment of troops from El Salvador, despite concerns that the outside intervention may worsen instability in the Caribbean country.
On Tuesday, hundreds of protesters rallied in the streets of cities like the capital, Port-au-Prince, bearing signs with slogans like “Down with the gangs”.
Haiti has long struggled with gang violence, but the crisis worsened around 2021, after the assassination of President Jovenel Moise. His death further weakened Haiti’s central government, and experts say gangs took advantage of the eroding public confidence to expand their influence.
The October 18 kidnapping of four Salvadoran aviation technicians near Port-au-Prince prompted El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele to respond with a military operation to Haiti.
But on Monday, El Salvador confirmed it would end its deployment of about 2,500 troops once the missing Salvadoran airmen were found.
“If they reappear tomorrow, as President Bukele said, we will leave,” Salvadoran Security Minister Gustavo Villatoro said.
That announcement, however, was followed by public gestures of support and diplomatic engagements, with some top officials in Haiti encouraging the Salvadoran deployment to stay.
Haitian Justice Minister Patrick Pelissier travelled to San Salvador on Monday and expressed gratitude for the troop surge.
“The Haitian people applaud the decision of Nayib Bukele to send troops,” Pelissier said on Monday.
He added that Haitian security forces, together with their international counterparts, had recently managed to regain control of Haiti’s national football stadium, held by gangs for years.
“During the operation, we discovered several human skulls inside the stadium,” Bukele claimed in a social media post last week.
The timeline for the Salvadoran troop withdrawal is uncertain. While El Salvador has framed its deployment as a rescue mission, the leader of Haiti’s 400 Mawozo gang, Wilson Joseph, told The Associated Press that the four technicians are already dead.
Joseph added that the abduction took place in territory controlled by Chen Mechan, a rival gang. He provided no evidence to back his assertions.
Bukele, however, has championed his country’s role in confronting Haiti’s gangs, using social media to promote the offensive and sharing videos of military operations.
The Salvadoran president — who once referred to himself as the “world’s coolest dictator” — has been credited with popularising a “mano dura” or “strong hand” approach to regional security.
Faced with one of the highest homicide rates in the world, Bukele launched a hardline security crackdown on gangs in El Salvador in 2022, including mass arrests and mass trials.
His heavy-handed approach has led to a sharp decline in crime but has also been widely condemned for human rights abuses.
Critics have warned that transplanting such tactics to Haiti could spark a backlash, leading to greater instability and risks to civilians.
They have also criticised the lack of long-term planning for El Salvador’s troop deployment; a sudden withdrawal, for instance, could worsen the situation for Haiti’s security forces.
Bukele is campaigning for a third term in El Salvador’s February presidential election, and analysts speculate his actions in Haiti could be used as a campaign tool to drum up support.
The Salvadoran deployment is the latest in a series of international interventions in Haiti.
Such foreign involvement is often controversial. The United States, for instance, has sent troops to Haiti on multiple occasions in the 20th century, occupying the country for decades and seizing control of its central bank.
More recently, a United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) arrived in Haiti in April, to help address the widespread gang violence.
Gangs control more than 80 percent of the capital region. The conflict has killed more than 22,000 people since 2022. UN reports attribute more than half of the deaths in the first nine months of the year to security operations, including the deaths of 300 civilians.
The UN also says almost 2,000 people have been displaced since the arrival of Salvadoran troops.
But Pelissier said Haiti’s government had not reported any civilian casualties in the latest operations, which he described as professional.
“The best to do is to avoid, as much as possible, human rights violations, and that’s what we are doing together,” the minister said.

articles.title_orig: Trump is trying to put the Iran war behind him, but it’s not over
articles.title_zh: Trump is trying to put the Iran war behind him, but it’s not over

Earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump faced a menu of war options and pushed them all aside. He also turned down the negotiated package on the table. Instead, he chose to keep tightening the screws on Iran through an economic blockade. Yet, rumors that he has shelved the military option or is warming to a deal are hasty. The more probable outcome is that he neither ends the conflict nor resolves it, but quietly drifts away from it while gradually loosening the blockade on Iran.
Pressure on Trump to restart the war has intensified dramatically since the midterms. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu knows that several factors will limit Trump’s ability to resume military action against Iran. First, Netanyahu may have only a few weeks left as Israel’s caretaker. If Gadi Eisenkot succeeds in forming a government in the next few weeks, Netanyahu will lose the premiership and his long-term dream of crushing the Iranian state. A rising chorus of former and current Israeli officials—from Avigdor Lieberman to Ehud Barak—are sounding the alarms that, out of desperation, Netanyahu is planning to “carry out a blatant military provocation in order to force Iran to respond on a scale triggering a war that would disrupt or prevent the establishment of a new government [in Israel].” The next Israeli prime minister will likely not share Netanyahu’s obsession with Iran or his skills in maneuvering the U.S. political system.

A rising chorus of former and current Israeli officials—from Avigdor Lieberman to Ehud Barak—are sounding the alarms that, out of desperation, Netanyahu is planning to “carry out a blatant military provocation in order to force Iran to respond on a scale triggering a war that would disrupt or prevent the establishment of a new government [in Israel].” The next Israeli prime minister will likely not share Netanyahu’s obsession with Iran or his skills in maneuvering the U.S. political system.
Second, in two months’ time, Trump’s maneuverability will be eclipsed by a Democratic Congress that can defund the war. Third, though U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth survived an impeachment attempt last week, his political future still hangs by a thread.
Even if the risk of war declines, this does not guarantee a greater likelihood of a deal. Key obstacles—including Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile, the future of its enrichment program, a regional cease-fire, sanctions relief, and the political cost for Trump—make both reaching and maintaining an agreement challenging.
The most likely scenario may turn out to be neither war nor peace, yet something altogether different from the economic blockade “middle path” that Trump chose earlier. In this scenario, Trump’s economic warfare and blockade would end up little more than words on paper. Trump would declare victory, reject both war and peace, withdraw the U.S. military, step away from the table, and insist that the blockade and sanctions remain in place while quietly allowing them to fade into irrelevance.
This would set in motion a gradual loosening of the blockade, with sanctions enforcement quietly eroding. Bit by bit, Asian and Middle Eastern countries would ramp up trade and investment in Iran, far surpassing current levels. Out of this slow transformation, a delicate new equilibrium would take shape: Sanctions enforcement would remain just robust enough for the United States to insist the system is intact, yet lax enough to persuade Tehran not to upset the emerging status quo.
This Swiss-cheese scenario is the only walk-away option that could work. If Trump truly keeps the blockade and sanctions in place, then the United States and Iran would be locked in a relentless standoff, always teetering on the edge of conflict, just as they are now. This fragile balance would inevitably tip into another war, completely undermining the whole point of walking away.
To be clear, the Swiss-cheese scenario is suboptimal compared with a peace deal. A peace deal that would end 47 years of enmity, uphold nonproliferation goals, open the Iranian economy to U.S. companies, and stabilize the region would far better serve U.S. interests. But the walk-away option carries the benefit, from Trump’s perspective, of avoiding an agreement that would manifest the failure of his war, as the Islamabad Memorandum did in the view of its critics. He will find it attractive because his focus is no longer on how much he can get, but how much he can avoid giving.
Indeed, the Swiss-cheese option guarantees that, while none of the sides walks away with a complete victory, everyone sidesteps their worst nightmare. Trump escapes both a humiliating compromise and the quagmire of another needless war. Tehran, in turn, dodges the devastation that a joint U,S. and Israeli assault on its vital infrastructure and energy lifelines would unleash. And given the shift in favor of nuclear weapons among the Iranian public, Iranian decision-makers may also welcome de facto partial sanctions relief without having to give up their stockpile of enriched uranium or give other nuclear concessions.
Even Israel might breathe easier, since its worst fear—a U.S.-Iran diplomatic breakthrough that could see old enemies reconcile—remains off the table, while the possibility of a future U.S.-Iran conflict still lingers. Israeli leaders will certainly view any loosening of the sanctions pressure as a loss, but it is still superior to a deal that undoes the sanctions architecture altogether. Moreover, Israel may calculate that the scenario still offers plenty of opportunities to tighten the sanctions or even escalate matters toward war.
In short, it’s neither side’s worst option, and everyone’s least-costly scenario.
And while Israel may still hope for chances to escalate, the Swiss-cheese scenario could turn out to be unexpectedly resilient, even as it leaves the U.S.-Iran conflict unresolved. Should this uneasy balance persist until 2029, the next U.S. president will stand at a crossroads: reignite tensions in pursuit of a better deal or quietly embrace the status quo and turn attention to the many other pressing crises on the United States’ plate. To most presidents, this will be a rather simple choice.
Given Trump’s refusal to admit defeat, his dread of looking like a loser, his allergy to tangled diplomacy, his fixation on eclipsing former U.S. President Barak Obama’s Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, and Iran’s refusal to offer him an ego-saving escape, Trump may ultimately declare a false victory and settle for the Swiss-cheese walk-away—not because it’s the smarter move but because it’s the cheapest way out.

articles.title_orig: Fed Minutes Show Almost All Officials Expect More Rate Hikes
articles.title_zh: Fed Minutes Show Almost All Officials Expect More Rate Hikes
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve officials expressed confidence in October that further interest rate increases will be needed to stem inflation, though they decided to hold off while gathering more information, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday.
Policymakers put artificial intelligence at the core of their discussions, indicating that demand associated with the technology would be "a material source of inflation risk."
More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple of participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December.
The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective."
In a CNBC interview Wednesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller reiterated his belief that the Federal Open Market Committee should consider a half-point hike in December.
Officials at the meeting expressed a high level of concern over AI, both as a source of inflation and financial instability.
Fed staff members who briefed participants noted "that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint."
"Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures," the minutes said. "A few participants remarked that AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms."
Officials said they still expect inflation to fall off sharply in 2027 and beyond as the impact from the current shocks wear off.
Ultimately, the FOMC voted 10-2 to keep its benchmark overnight borrowing rate locked in a range between 3.75%-4%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase.
Those voting in favor of the hold "pointed to benefits in accumulating additional information, which would help in determining the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
Since the meeting, the inflation data has shown that the pace of price increases remains well above target.
The consumer price index in October rose 0.4% for all items and 0.3% for the core that excludes food and energy. Both readings were 0.1 percentage point higher than expected.
While indicating concern over how stubborn inflation has been, most Fed officials who have spoken publicly advocated a patient approach.
However, Waller said Wednesday that the Fed may have to "shock" markets by approving a half-point hike in December. He is the only central banker to espouse that belief publicly, though St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said he anticipates as much as a full percentage point move higher by the spring of 2027. As governor, Waller is a permanent FOMC voter; Musalem will not vote until 2028.
Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Friday on CNBC that the central bank risks losing its credibility if it doesn't act.
At the core of policymakers' concern is whether rising prices related to the Iran war and President Donald Trump 's tariffs, in many cases temporary events that wouldn't prompt a response, are instead becoming more entrenched.
Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting that includes low odds of a half-point move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Futures traders also are pricing a solid likelihood of two more increases in 2027.

articles.title_orig: FAA chief urges critics to ‘lay off’ Sean Duffy for flight stoppage: ‘Blame me’
articles.title_zh: FAA chief urges critics to ‘lay off’ Sean Duffy for flight stoppage: ‘Blame me’
articles.content_orig:
Bryan Bedford’s comments come as Duffy, Trump transport secretary, faces scrutiny over handling of outage crisis
The head of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) took responsibility for the nationwide ground stop that affected more than 12,400 flights on Friday, urging people to “lay off” Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary.
“I take full responsibility for it,” Bryan Bedford, the FAA administrator, said at an aviation event staged by the Hill on Wednesday.
“I wish people would lay off the secretary,” Bedford added. “He’s got a lot of work to do, but I’m the guy they hired to get this done. So blame me if we need to blame somebody. Blame me.”
The FAA administrator’s comments arrived as Duffy, the top transportation official in the US, faces scrutiny from former officials and lawmakers over his handling of the tech outage crisis, which left tens of thousands of travelers stranded over the weekend.
In a press conference on Friday, Duffy refused to accept responsibility or apologize for the crisis, blaming Democratic lawmakers and his predecessors for not providing the funding to upgrade outdated systems.
The FAA said it grounded all flights after a newly installed router flooded communication systems, causing problems between aircraft systems and radar feeds.
Trump administration officials have emphasized that the tech outage at the FAA was not caused by a cybersecurity attack and was unrelated to other disruptions.
Jay Clayton, director of national intelligence, testified on Wednesday that there was no indication the outage was the result of a malicious actor or connected to similar disruptions that have affected banks and major companies. He said the outages were caused by patches – modifications to systems to address issues such as security vulnerabilities.
But lawmakers, including some Republicans, have grown frustrated with Duffy after he and the White House asked Congress to provide $50bn in funding to upgrade the air traffic system, more than double what was originally estimated.
Some GOP lawmakers told reporters the justification behind the large sum of money was thin.
But Bedford argued the investment was necessary on Wednesday, claiming Donald Trump and Duffy believed the outage was a “call to action” to “fix the system” and “return to the gold standard”.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia interim CEO Kress tells employees ‘let’s move forward’ at first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang exit
articles.title_zh: Nvidia interim CEO Kress tells employees ‘let’s move forward’ at first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang exit
articles.content_orig:
Humilis Investment Strategies CEO and CIO Brian Belski joins Taylor Riggs to analyze Nvidia's third-quarter earnings beat, showing a 103% year-over-year revenue surge. They also discuss the board's decision regarding Jensen Huang.
Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday's earnings call that the company is well-positioned to move forward following the abrupt resignation of co-founder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang last week following the revelation of extramarital affairs.
Kress, who has served as Nvidia's CFO since 2013, delivered the AI giant's first quarterly earnings report since Huang's departure, which beat the market's expectations in terms of revenue and earnings per share.
"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this," Kress said on the call.
"With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia's leadership position," she added.
NVIDIA RELEASES QUARTERLY EARNINGS, SUGGESTS FUTURE PLANS AFTER JENSEN HUANG'S RESIGNATION
Nvidia's quarterly earnings beat the market's expectations in its first report since Jensen Huang's resignation. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Investors were looking for the company to provide reassurance about its path forward as well as to post strong results over the prior three months in what was viewed as a test for the durability of the AI trade .
Nvidia's earnings beat analysts' estimates for quarterly revenue , which came in at $115.8 billion and topped the estimate of $109.1 billion reflected in data compiled by LSEG. Diluted earnings per share were $2.68, beating the estimate of $2.48.
Revenue was up 20% on a quarterly basis and 103% year over year, while earnings per share rose 10% from the prior quarter and 108% from a year ago. Nvidia's net income for the quarter was $65.3 billion, which represents a quarterly increase of 9% and a rise of 105% year over year.
Nvidia lifted its forecast for the fourth quarter of its fiscal 2027, which includes an additional week, to project $130 billion in revenue, plus or minus 3%; while Kress said the company raised its fiscal year 2028 outlook with revenue growth of 75% year over year, an increase from 70%.
JENSEN HUANG SAYS HE IS WILLING TO RETURN AS NVIDIA CEO, SAYING 'I OWN MY MISTAKES COMPLETELY'
Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO. (Nvidia/Handout)
She also noted that Nvidia's cloud industry backlog grew to $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just three months ago, which underscored the "significant multiyear opportunity ahead of our partners and of Nvidia."
Earlier on Tuesday before the earnings release, Huang released a statement saying that "I own my mistakes completely" and that he would be open to returning as the company's CEO if the board of directors thought it would be "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America."
Harvey Jones, chairman of the Nvidia board of directors, shut down that speculation on the earnings call, saying that Huang voluntarily resigned and the board "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
NVIDIA ADDS BOARD OVERSIGHT OF NATIONAL SECURITY AND EXPORT COMPLIANCE
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang said Tuesday he would be willing to return as CEO after resigning last week, though the board chairman later said directors don't plan to do so. (Soeren Stache/picture alliance via Getty Images)
The chairman said that the company will consider internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent CEO. He added that while the board would like to name the permanent CEO soon, it isn't in a rush to do so and "won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person."
Jones also praised Kress, saying that "Colette has been at the center of this company's extraordinary growth for the last 13 years, instrumental in executing strategy and with a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position."

Prince Harry is forcing himself back into the royal limelight with headline-grabbing antics in a war-torn country, a top royal journalist alleges.
As his popularity continues to wane back home, the Duke of Sussex made a surprise visit Sunday to the Superhuman Center rehabilitation clinic in Lviv, Ukraine, where he fraternized with injured soldiers and assured them they will âwinâ the war with Russia.
âEvery single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth. Youâre going to win the war, and then youâre going to be set up for success,â Harry said at the event.
Harry told Ukrainian soldiers that the United Kingdom has their back.
Efrem Lukatsky/Efrem Lukatsky/via REUTERS
However, former Page Six deputy editor and news commentator Paula Froelich tells The Royalist that she believes the highly publicized trip was another case of Harryâs âattention dependency disorder,â rather than a gesture of actual goodwill.
âIf he doesnât get a headline or heâs not in the paper at least three or four times a week, the poor guy starts to fade away like heâs invisible and doesnât know what to do,â Froelich said. âYou got plenty of veterans at home who need your help, and he ainât paying attention to them.â
Harryâs trip to the east also coincided with Prince William and Princess Catherineâs trip to Mumbai, India, for the Earthshot Prize Awards, a global initiative founded by the next-in-line that awards winners prizes around $1.3 million dollars to bolster environmental solutions.
William and Catherine attended the Earthshot Awards in Mumbai, India on Sunday.
Phil Noble/Phil Noble/REUTERS
âTo put yourself in a position where it looks like you are trying to steal the thunder from an environmental NGOâ¦ just seems so incredibly crass,â The Royalist host Tom Sykes said. âIt just feels like a sort of angry child stamping their feet and going, âLook at me, look at me, look at me,â doesnât it?â
In the public eye, Harryâs friends have maintained that there is no estrangement between him and King Charles. The Sussex couple recently announced that theyâd be staying in England over the holidays, but Sykes suggested it may have something to do with Meghanâs father, Thomas Markle Sr., being arrested in Florida on child pornography charges.
Meghan's father, Thomas Markle, has been arrested on child pornography charges in Florida.
Pinellas County Sheriff's Office/Pinellas County Sheriff's Office/Handout/via REUTERS
âNow theyâre saying theyâre staying here,â Sykes said. âPeople canât help thinking itâs not completely unconnected to developments in Meghanâs family, specifically the orange jumpsuit that her father was photographed wearing the other day.â
In the wake of revelations about her father, Sykes said Meghan has appeared âhauntedâ by her lack of control over the narrative.
âSomething has obviously really massively changed,â Sykes said. âShe looks genuinely like not in control of the situationâ¦ And now weâve got sort of Harry trying to pretend itâs business as usual.â
Froelich said that she was surprised to see such emotional imagery of Meghan, considering she has reportedly known about her fatherâs situation for the last several years.
âSheâs leaning into the role of grief store in chief,â Froelich said. âHeâs leaning into the role of âIâve got your back, soldiers,â when, of course, he only really has his own back.â

articles.title_orig: One of AI's most notorious 'doomers' stands to make billions in Anthropic's IPO
articles.title_zh: One of AI's most notorious 'doomers' stands to make billions in Anthropic's IPO
articles.content_orig:
An Estonian tech billionaire famous for his stance that AI could end humanity is expected to be one of the biggest winners in Anthropic's upcoming IPO .
Jaan Tallinn co-founded Skype and later sold it to eBay . He led Anthropic's first funding round, a $124 million Series A, five years ago — well before the company's Claude chatbot was on the market and took Wall Street and Silicon Valley by storm.
Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT in what could be the largest IPO of all time, and the first public debut for an AI lab.
Tallinn's exact holdings haven't been disclosed. But given Anthropic's expected debut valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion, the return on his initial investment could be well into the tens of billions. His exact return would depend on the level of dilution in subsequent funding rounds and whether he sold any shares along the way.
Anthropic's earliest backers connected with the company through philanthropic circles worried about AI's existential risk. They're sometimes described as "doomers."
In 2020, Tallinn told CNBC that there's a 1-in-6 chance that humans won't survive this century, referencing a book from Oxford professor Toby Ord. Tallinn also described a runaway AI scenario where a model is left working overnight and "the world is no longer there in the morning."
While he continued to work in tech, Tallinn co-founded the Cambridge Centre for the Study of Existential Risk and the Future of Life Institute , known for one of the first public calls to pause AI. Despite high-profile signatories , including Elon Musk and Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak, the institute's "Pause Giant AI Experiments" letter in 2023 had little effect on the industry.
Tallinn's view on AI was influenced by researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky, who co-authored the 2025 book "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies," about the catastrophic risk of AI without proper checks, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Tallinn, who has an estimated net worth of more than $10 billion, later crossed paths with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who had defected from OpenAI with his eventual co-founders, citing views that Sam Altman's company wasn't taking AI safety seriously enough.
Amodei and Tallinn overlapped in the effective altruism community, according to people who know both of them. Effective altruism, sometimes known as EA , is a philosophy that aims to use data and evidence to maximize philanthropic impact. While there's no official membership, its Silicon Valley network ended up generating much of Anthropic's early venture capital money, according to multiple people.
Tallinn's early bet was that bankrolling a safety-conscious AI company was one of the best ways to keep a lid on the risk, these people said. Tallinn also invested in DeepMind, which was later acquired by Google .
One person, who asked not to be named, said that at the time of Tallinn's investment, there was no expectation that Anthropic "would be a profitable undertaking." Venture investors hadn't yet gone all-in on AI, and it was "before the era of putting AI in your pitch deck," said the person, who asked not to be named in order to speak candidly on the matter.
Tallinn declined to be interviewed for this story.
Anthropic's first round in 2021 also included Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz, who founded Open Philanthropy — now known as Coefficient Giving — which is deeply rooted in effective altruism. The charity was co-founded by Holden Karnofsky, husband of Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei. Karnofsky also started GiveWell, also largely tied to effective altruism.
Former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried, another known effective altruist, backed Anthropic in its early days alongside Tallinn. Bankman-Fried participated in the Series B in 2022 through his now-defunct hedge fund Alameda Research. The former CEO was convicted of fraud in 2023 and sentenced to 25 years in prison. His stake was sold in bankruptcy auction at a fraction of the company's current valuation.
Tallinn's early investment initially put Anthropic's price tag at $461 million, according to Pitchbook. It has ballooned in value since, and last raised money at a $965 billion valuation in private markets. The lab has raised money from tech giants Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Nvidia, and plans to sell $26 billion worth of shares to a group of tech companies at the IPO price.
Anthropic's early investors and some in the safety community aren't overwhelmingly cheering the IPO. Many worry behind the scenes that AI safety will take a back seat to Anthropic's commercial success and wider shareholder base, according to a person close to the group.
Many in the AI safety community "are opposed to the IPO," this person said.
Others point to Anthropic's unique corporate structure that gives the founders broad discretion and control of the company through a single super-voting share. The co-founders will be sole members of "Founder LLC," which will hold 50.1% of the voting power. But Anthropic is also built as a public benefit corporation, meaning it has a dual mandate beyond just a duty to shareholders. It has to serve the best interests of its "company purpose" to facilitate the "responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."

articles.title_orig: Israeli tanks roll into central Gaza in first ground operation since ceasefire began
articles.title_zh: Israeli tanks roll into central Gaza in first ground operation since ceasefire began
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of displaced Palestinians fled their tents and shelters in central ‌Gaza on Wednesday as Israeli tanks advanced, in what the Israeli military said was an operation targeting Hamas infrastructure outside areas that Israel controls in ⁠the enclave.
Witnesses said some Israeli tanks rolled onto the main Salahudeen road, west of the Yellow Line that marks the boundary of the two-thirds of the Gaza Strip still under Israeli control despite ⁠a ceasefire that has ​lasted more ⁠than a year.
An Israeli airstrike near the army raid killed one person, Palestinian medics said.
The medics ⁠said separate Israeli airstrikes had killed two other people ​earlier ⁠in the day in ‌ Deir al-Balah and Gaza City.
An Israeli military spokesperson told NBC News that the military was carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of ‌the Yellow Line in central Gaza ‌and that it had struck a militant in southern Gaza earlier on Wednesday.
They later confirmed that it was the first ground operation since the U.S. brokered ceasefire came into effect in October 2025 .
Dozens of Palestinians, most of whom have been displaced multiple times since the start of the war in 2023, piled their belongings on top of bicycles, wheelchairs, motorcycles and vehicles as ​they fled the area.
Salam Aql said the military had ordered residents of the area to leave “but we wanted to stay because we ​are exhausted from being displaced so many times.”
“We are tired, I swear to God, we are tired. But as we were sitting there, gunfire started ‌coming ⁠in,” she said, adding that a boy was hit in the leg by a bullet.
“Once he was wounded, we could not stay any longer.”
Hamas said the Israeli military’s raid and forced displacement of Palestinians marked a ceasefire violation and a ​dangerous escalation.
The truce halted major fighting in the Israel-Gaza war, although it has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas’ disarmament.
The Israeli military spokesperson had no immediate comment on other strikes.
Residents reported hearing tank shells being fired in the area. An Israeli airstrike near the location of the army raid killed one person, Palestinian medics said.
Israel, which says Hamas has recently been regrouping and rearming, has stepped up attacks against the Islamist group. Hamas has accused Israel of attempting to derail the U.S.-brokered ceasefire agreement.
Gaza health ‌authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been ​killed since the ceasefire went into effect, while ‌the Israeli military says five Israeli soldiers have been killed.
Palestinian authorities say more ⁠than 74,000 people in Gaza have been killed in the military campaign ‌that Israel ​launched there after Hamas-led fighters killed ‌about 1,200 people in southern ​Israel in an attack on October 7, 2023.
The body overseeing US President Donald Trump’s plan to end the Gaza war on Wednesday ​accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to meet their commitments to end hostilities, leaving the population of Gaza in dire conditions and the ‌ceasefire in danger of collapse.
The 12-page Board of Peace report, seen by Reuters, is the body’s second to the United Nations Security Council since the US-backed ceasefire came into effect 13 months ago. It offers a sobering assessment of progress made since then.
The board, established and headed by Trump, is expected to present the report’s findings to a meeting of the council in New York at ​the end of November.
“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” ​the report said, warning that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely.”
While the ceasefire has halted major ⁠fighting, the wider plan, which calls for Hamas to disarm, Israeli troops to withdraw and reconstruction to begin, has effectively stalled since soon after it came into effect ​last year.
Hamas agreed in July to a Board of Peace roadmap to surrender its weapons and transfer governance of Gaza to a civilian transitional authority, but Israel rejected the ​roadmap, saying it will not withdraw until Hamas is dismantled.
Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza, while the report said Hamas fighters have also continued attacks on Israeli troops.
“Every day that Israel continues strikes against Hamas targets, it delays putting Hamas’ agreement to the roadmap to the test,” the report said.
“Meanwhile, Hamas militant activity continues, the commitment to cease all military activities has not ​been met in full by the parties, and the population faces another winter in tents and rubble.”
Senior Hamas official Basem Naim dismissed the report as “pure disinformation”, accusing the ​Board of Peace of providing cover to Israel to evade its commitments under the plan to end the war and to continue its aggression in Gaza.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister ‌Benjamin Netanyahu ⁠and a spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Chantal Da Silva reports on world news for NBC News Digital and is based in London.

articles.title_orig: Denmark’s oldest-ever person, 112, outed as one-time ‘prominent’ Nazi leader
articles.title_zh: Denmark’s oldest-ever person, 112, outed as one-time ‘prominent’ Nazi leader
articles.content_orig:
Denmark’s oldest living person, 112-year-old Kirsten Schwalbe, held two local leadership positions in the Danish Nazi party during the German occupation, according to documents reviewed by Frihedsbrevet.
Records from the Danish National Archives show that Schwalbe served as acting branch group leader and women’s group leader for the party’s Holstebro branch from August 1943 to July 1944.
Her husband also served as acting branch leader in Holstebro from November 1942 to July 1944.
The documents do not describe Schwalbe’s specific duties or the extent of her work. However, two historians who examined the records told Frihedsbrevet that her positions went beyond ordinary party membership.
Schwalbe previously confirmed that she had joined the party but said she did so at her husband’s urging. She denied having sided with the German occupying forces.
Her family said she was deeply affected by the renewed coverage and was unable to comment. They have asked the media to respect her health and privacy.
Publisher Gyldendal recently released a biography of Schwalbe without knowing about the leadership roles. Publishing director Mette Korsgaard said the information changed the book’s premise and must be examined before the publisher decides its future.
Historian Gry Scavenius Bertelsen said Denmark must address aspects of its wartime history that challenge familiar national narratives.
Denmark faces a cold and unsettled week, with rain and clouds potentially giving way to sleet and snow later in the week.
Sandra Nygaard, a meteorologist at the Danish Meteorological Institute, said Thursday and Friday could feel increasingly wintry, with overnight frost also expected.
Monday will be cloudy with light rain across most of the country. Western areas may see some sunshine later in the day. Temperatures will range from 5 to 10 degrees Celsius, with strong winds possible along the coasts.
Northern and eastern Denmark will remain cloudy with some rain Tuesday, while other areas may initially see sunshine. Temperatures will range from 4 to 8 degrees.
Wednesday will bring clouds and rain, particularly in southern Denmark, with temperatures between 3 and 8 degrees.
Rain could turn to sleet or snow in some places Thursday as temperatures fall to between freezing and 6 degrees. Southern and eastern areas currently appear most likely to experience wintry precipitation, although the forecast remains uncertain.
Similar conditions are expected Friday, with periods of sunshine, rain and potentially sleet or snow.
Several low-pressure systems moving in from the west and southwest are causing the unsettled weather. Drier conditions are expected during the weekend.
Denmark and four other European Union countries are negotiating an agreement to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, according to Danish broadcaster DR.
Denmark is working with Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece on plans for a return center outside the EU.
Danish Immigration Minister Morten Bødskov said the government would initially focus on rejected asylum seekers rather than foreign nationals ordered to leave Denmark after criminal convictions.
“We are looking at a group of around 100,” Bødskov said. “They take up space in our centers, and we will start with them.”
The plans are expected to be presented Monday at a migration conference in Vienna, Austria.
Efforts to establish a return center outside the EU have been underway for several years.
An EU regulation adopted in June allows member countries to establish return centers outside the bloc for people whose asylum applications have been rejected.
Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece have since led efforts to reach an agreement.
It remains unclear what Rwanda would receive in return for accepting the rejected asylum seekers.
Denmark’s oldest living person, 112-year-old Kirsten Schwalbe, held two local leadership positions in the Danish Nazi party during the German occupation, according to documents reviewed by Frihedsbrevet.
Records from the Danish National Archives show that Schwalbe served as acting branch group leader and women’s group leader for the party’s Holstebro branch from August 1943 to July 1944.
Her husband also served as acting branch leader in Holstebro from November 1942 to July 1944.
The documents do not describe Schwalbe’s specific duties or the extent of her work. However, two historians who examined the records told Frihedsbrevet that her positions went beyond ordinary party membership.
Schwalbe previously confirmed that she had joined the party but said she did so at her husband’s urging. She denied having sided with the German occupying forces.
Her family said she was deeply affected by the renewed coverage and was unable to comment. They have asked the media to respect her health and privacy.
Publisher Gyldendal recently released a biography of Schwalbe without knowing about the leadership roles. Publishing director Mette Korsgaard said the information changed the book’s premise and must be examined before the publisher decides its future.
Historian Gry Scavenius Bertelsen said Denmark must address aspects of its wartime history that challenge familiar national narratives.
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen has rejected a reported US proposal linking Ukrainian concessions in the Donbas region to NATO membership.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that US negotiators had asked whether Ukraine would surrender Donbas in exchange for joining the military alliance.
“It is completely upside down,” Løkke said, arguing that negotiations must begin with an unconditional ceasefire.
He said Russian President Vladimir Putin remained maximalist in his demands and criticized the suggestion that Russia should receive territory it has failed to conquer during almost five years of war.
Løkke also rejected discussing Europe’s future security architecture with Russia before a peace agreement is reached, describing the issue as premature.
However, he said Europe should still participate when discussions take place, as European representatives did on the sidelines of recent talks in Abu Dhabi.
“It is important that there is dialogue and contact,” Løkke said. “It just must not be confused with peace negotiations. They will only come when the parties are ready.”
According to Løkke, Ukraine, Europe and the United States are prepared to accept an unconditional ceasefire, while Russia is not.
He therefore said the conditions for formal peace negotiations do not currently exist.
Travelers should expect delays and cancellations across parts of Denmark’s rail network from Monday morning because of an unusually high number of track defects.
Regional trains between Odense and Fredericia will be replaced by buses in both directions. Intercity trains will continue to operate but are expected to face delays of about 15 minutes on the main route connecting Copenhagen, Funen and Fredericia.
DSB, Denmark’s national rail operator, said trains must reduce their speed to around 80 kilometers per hour on affected sections, compared with normal speeds of up to 180 kilometers per hour.
Speed restrictions will also affect several routes on Zealand.
Trains between Copenhagen and Næstved will operate only between Køge Nord and Næstved. Passengers traveling between Køge Nord and Copenhagen can use the S-train network.
Express services between Helsingør and Copenhagen will be canceled during rush hour.
Banedanmark, the state agency responsible for Denmark’s rail infrastructure, said it has identified 50 percent more rail defects than during a normal year.
The temporary timetable is expected to remain in effect until November 29, when authorities will assess whether normal services can resume.
Passengers are encouraged to check Rejseplanen before traveling. Those delayed by more than 30 minutes can apply to DSB for compensation under its travel-time guarantee.

articles.title_orig: The first Nvidia RTX Spark mini PCs launch today from Asus, Dell, and MSI
articles.title_zh: The first Nvidia RTX Spark mini PCs launch today from Asus, Dell, and MSI
articles.content_orig:
New NVIDIA RTX Spark compact desktops from ASUS, Dell and MSI are available today, bringing local AI agents, image and video generation, and model fine-tuning to a dedicated Windows PC.
With up to 128GB of unified memory and NVIDIA’s AI software stack, these systems provide room for larger local models alongside RTX-accelerated creative and development tools. A dedicated desktop can keep agents and scheduled tasks running while a laptop travels or handles other work.
Alongside the new desktops, an expanding software ecosystem brings more creative and development workflows to RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops.
Native Windows on Arm applications from Adobe, the NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction feature in Blender and local generation workflows in ComfyUI expand what creators and developers can do on RTX Spark — all on one Windows PC.
As workflows expand to include local AI models and agents, more work can continue beyond an active editing session — from generating assets to processing long renders or scheduled tasks.
RTX Spark compact desktops give developers, creators and AI enthusiasts a dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents. They bring together image and video generation, model fine-tuning, creative applications and development tools in one compact system.
Running supported models locally keeps locally processed code and files on the PC and avoids per-token cloud application programming interface (API) charges for those tasks.
RTX Spark desktops are equipped with a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores and up to 128GB of unified memory, delivering up to 1 petaflop of AI performance. Ten-gigabit Ethernet connectivity enables fast transfers of large datasets, model files and creative assets between RTX Spark compact desktops and networked storage.
This advanced hardware unlocks incredible capabilities for creators, developers and AI enthusiasts, including:
New compact desktops are available for purchase from ASUS, Dell and MSI, joining the RTX Spark family of laptops available today. Mini PCs from Acer, GIGABYTE and HP are coming soon, along with the Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box .
Native CUDA support and Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux give developers a foundation for building and running local AI workflows. Developers can set up agents with Hermes Agent or NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and fine-tune supported models using Unsloth.
RTX Spark can run creative agents that connect familiar applications and local AI tools, helping creators move from an idea to finished work with natural-language instructions.
NVIDIA Switchyard, now available in Hermes, automatically routes agent tasks between local and cloud models. Everyday tasks can run on device, while advanced reasoning draws on cloud models, helping manage cloud costs across creative workflows.
These capabilities come together in creative workflows that connect Photoshop and ComfyUI through Hermes Agent. Using natural-language instructions, creators can turn sketches into rendered images and animations, or animate an image entirely on device — from isolating a subject and defining its motion to generating the finished video.
NVIDIA brought these workflows to life at Adobe MAX, where attendees used natural-language instructions to turn sketches into rendered images and animations for a shared digital Miami landscape.
The RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR features, already available in ComfyUI, extend the pipeline: a generated clip can be expanded to 60 frames per second and converted to high dynamic range for color grading, all within a single ComfyUI workflow on RTX Spark.
NVIDIA and Adobe are expanding native Windows on Arm support and RTX acceleration across Adobe’s creative applications, helping video editors, photographers, designers and 3D artists work more efficiently on RTX Spark.
Adobe Premiere accelerates a range of AI-powered editing features through NVIDIA TensorRT-RTX , including Enhance Speech, Object Mask, Scene Edit Detection and Auto Reframe — so editors spend less time waiting and more time cutting.
GPU acceleration also extends to Film Impact transition and effects plug-ins. The update improves support for professional video formats, including Canon RAW, Red RAW, ARRI RAW, ARRICORE, ARRI HDE, H.264 and HEVC in MXF, ProRes RAW and long-GOP video. This lets editors realize more than 50% quicker turnaround on everyday H.264 video deliverables.
Adobe Photoshop adds TensorRT-RTX acceleration for the Remove Tool and ArmRTX Spark-native Camera Raw support, helping photographers remove unwanted objects faster and work with RAW images without relying on emulation. At Adobe MAX, Adobe previewed a next-generation image processing engine with extensive GPU acceleration, including interactive Gaussian blur and Light Leaks filters.
Adobe Substance 3D Painter 12.2 is now optimized for RTX Spark with native support on Arm for the first time in public beta. Artists in games, visual effects and visualization can run Substance Painter natively on RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops, with no compatibility layer required.
Adobe Illustrator and InDesign now offer native Windows on Arm versions optimized for RTX Spark. Adobe Illustrator delivers up to 30% higher performance than its emulated version, helping accelerate illustration, graphic design and page-layout workflows on RTX Spark.
Blender 5.3 integrates DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction into the Cycles viewport, helping artists evaluate lighting and materials with near-final-quality ray-traced previews as they work.
The practical difference is immediate: instead of navigating a noisy, resolving preview, Ray Reconstruction delivers near-final-quality lighting, reflections and materials in the interactive viewport in real time.
DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support requires Blender 5.3 and the latest NVIDIA Game Ready Driver or NVIDIA Studio Driver. Download the NVIDIA App to get automatic notifications when the latest drivers are available, optimize games and applications from a unified GPU control center, and discover the latest NVIDIA tools and software.
Announced at Microsoft Ignite, Windows Server is evolving for organizations that need to run AI closer to their enterprise applications and data.
Microsoft is expanding hardware choice through support for the latest AI silicon, helping customers take advantage of accelerated inference and increasingly capable models in their own environments. NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows platform powered by the GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Desktop Superchip is expanding to include support for Windows Server 2028.
New accelerator platforms and the breadth of the Windows silicon ecosystem provide customers options at different capability levels and price points for advanced AI development, local inference, and agent workloads at scale.
Also announced at Microsoft Ignite, developers can now bring any GGUF model from Hugging Face and run it within Windows ML using the llama.cpp backend.
The DxCGC backend, now available as an experimental release, is an integration for game developers that compiles and runs machine learning models through DirectX 12, allowing them to execute AI workloads alongside graphics.
Windows APIs let applications integrate platform-provided AI capabilities adding GPU support for AION Instruct and VSR.
Developers can also build high-performance AI models for Windows ML using the command line interface.
