articles.title_orig: Ukraine Hits 2 Major Russian Refineries Again as Fuel Shortages Spread Across at Least 8 Regions
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Hits 2 Major Russian Refineries Again as Fuel Shortages Spread Across at Least 8 Regions
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Ukraine reportedly struck the Afipsky and Ilsky oil refineries in Russia’s Krasnodar Territory for the second time this month. The wider campaign has cut Russian crude processing by 30% and contributed to gasoline shortages and sales restrictions in at least eight regions.
Ukraine attacked two major oil refineries in Russia’s Krasnodar Territory overnight on Wednesday, Nov. 18, marking the second strike on both facilities this month, according to Ukrainian monitoring channels and Russian media reports.
A large-scale drone attack targeted the Seversky District of the Krasnodar Territory.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Debris from the drones sparked fires at two industrial facilities, while fragments were found at nine other locations, including private residential yards and streets, the region’s operational headquarters reported. Four people were injured and are receiving medical attention.
The Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ identified the facilities as the Afipsky and Ilsky oil refineries. Sources cited by the Russian independent outlet Astra also confirmed fires at both sites.
The Afipsky refinery is one of the three largest in the Krasnodar Territory and among the five largest in southern Russia. It can process more than 7 million tons of crude oil annually, producing gasoline, diesel fuel, jet fuel, and other petroleum products. The facility is focused exclusively on exports.
The Wednesday strike was the eighth attack on the Afipsky refinery since the beginning of the year and the second this month. It was last targeted by Ukrainian drones on Nov. 6.
The Ilsky refinery is also among the three largest in the Krasnodar Territory, with an annual crude oil processing capacity of approximately 6.6 million tons. It produces gasoline, diesel, and other petroleum products.
The facility was last targeted on Monday, when, according to Ukraine’s General Staff, three atmospheric crude distillation units were hit.
The Russian defense ministry said its air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 184 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones between 8 p.m. Moscow time on Tuesday and 8 a.m. on Wednesday.
According to the ministry, the drones were intercepted over the Belgorod and Rostov regions, Krasnodar Krai, Crimea, and the Sea of Azov.
Ukraine’s General Staff later confirmed that two oil refineries had been struck.
“Ukraine’s Defense Forces launched an aerial attack on the Ilsky and Afipsky oil refineries – two key fuel suppliers in southern Russia,” the General Staff said in a statement published on Telegram.
As per the report, explosions and smoke were observed near the Ilsky refinery, where storage tanks were hit.
Preliminary information indicates that an oil processing unit was struck at the Afipsky refinery. The facility has an annual processing capacity of 6.25 million tons, accounting for more than 2% of Russia’s total oil refining capacity.
The General Staff said the two refineries have a combined annual processing capacity of approximately 13 million tons of oil.
“Located in the south, they serve as the shortest supply route for fuel to Russian forces at the front. Therefore, every fire at these facilities means less diesel and gasoline for the Russian army, and fewer ‘oil-rubles’ – funds the Russian aggressor uses to purchase missiles and Shahed drones,” the statement said.
“Exercising their right to self-defense, as guaranteed by Article 51 of the UN Charter, Ukraine’s Defense Forces continue to take systematic measures to compel Russia to cease its armed aggression against Ukraine,” it added.
Kyiv resumed its campaign against Russian oil refineries in late October. Over the past few weeks, Ukrainian forces have struck around 10 of Russia’s 35 refineries, including facilities in Novokuibyshevsk, Ryazan, Afipsky, Saratov, Yaroslavl, Omsk, Nizhny Novgorod, Ufa, and Kirishi.
The attacks have contributed to a sharp decline in Russia’s oil refining volumes. Refineries were processing approximately 700,000 metric tons (5 million barrels) of crude oil per day at the end of October, but that figure had fallen to around 500,000 tons per day by mid-November – a reduction of about 30%, according to informed sources cited by Reuters.
The drop in refining capacity has also contributed to fuel shortages at gas stations in at least eight Russian regions, The Moscow Times reported .
Restrictions on gasoline sales have been introduced in the Leningrad, Nizhny Novgorod, Arkhangelsk, Novosibirsk, and Penza regions, as well as in the republics of Karelia and Buryatia.
In Moscow, Rosneft gas stations have reinstated purchase limits: Motorists can buy no more than 50 liters (13 gallons) of fuel per vehicle, while sales in canisters are capped at 20 liters.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

articles.title_zh: I watched Trump, Xi and Putin gather in China. Here are my top takeaways
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — It took a trip to China for me, an American, to see U.S. President Donald Trump in person for the first time.
Trump emerged from a group of black-clad photographers and other personnel surrounding him at a welcome banquet in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Leaders' Meeting held November 17th to 19th.
Seated just a few spots to his left was Russian President Vladimir Putin who picked up a glass of red wine to join a toast led by Chinese President Xi Jinping .
"At tomorrow's Leaders' Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual opening up, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, and identify opportunities to expand practical cooperation across various fields, so as to translate more initiatives into tangible results," Xi said in Mandarin, according to a CNBC translation.
Xi was speaking broadly, but Thursday's agenda includes a bilateral meeting with Trump, and their highly anticipated trilateral meeting with Putin.
But looking at the mood in the room, it seemed that their trilateral conversation had already started Wednesday night at their long banquet table. Much of what happens at APEC, including bilateral meetings and other exchanges between leaders, takes place away from the media.
But what struck me was how little sign there was of the tension surrounding Nvidia 's CEO Jensen Huang resignation, a controversy that has gripped markets for the past 10 days.
Ahead of Trump's entrance into the banquet hall, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao shared a friendly moment with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other members of the American delegation.
Last week, the U.S. officials said that Trump did not plan to raise allegations of Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy during his meeting with Xi.
It was a striking contrast to just two months ago, when I saw photographs of Huang and Tesla CEO Elon Musk sharing a table with Trump and Xi in Washington, D.C.
And when Trump visited Beijing in May, Huang took a few minutes to speak with reporters, including me, inside the Great Hall of the People. Musk was there too, accompanied by one of his sons.
This time, neither were visible in a room that was closely watched by the world. Musk was expected to join Trump's delegation in Shenzhen, but I did not see him Wednesday evening.
Their absence from the government-heavy banquet was striking. The world's most powerful leaders may be grappling with the implications of artificial intelligence, but they certainly didn't need the industry's biggest names at the table to do so.
China's Xi calls for removing trade and investment barriers
Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition
Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China
Over the months I've spent following APEC's "China Year," one thing has become clear: The forum has given Beijing an opportunity to host the U.S., Japan and other member economies at a time when unresolved tensions might otherwise have made such gatherings difficult.
But even in a year defined by talks of U.S.-China "strategic stability," the APEC events have exposed the rifts and the shifting dynamics in global power. Those dynamics were on display for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
Several hundred attendees, from Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun to U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue, arrived early for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
After waiting in silence for at least 10 minutes, the audience welcomed Xi in a distinctly modern way: by raising their smartphones to capture the moment. The applause was rather muted.
It was much the same at the more government-heavy welcome banquet that evening. So many attendees rushed to take their own photographs of Xi and other leaders entering the room that reporters' views were largely blocked.
Following Xi's morning speech, there was a lengthy intermission before Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim took the stage.
"The entire multilateral framework needs to change," he said, praising China on its "rare" recognition of smaller countries.
During the tea break that followed, attendees quickly resumed mingling. Some even brought coffee and snacks back into the room as Putin prepared to speak.
They listened as the Russian president talked about his country's economic resilience and claimed Europe was losing ground. As attendees headed to lunch, one thing stood out: Neither Trump nor any other G7 leader had taken the stage at the opening event. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke later in the afternoon.
The most visible American presence during the morning session came from business leaders appearing in a promotional video ahead of Xi's speech.
And the absence of an American voice was perhaps even more noticeable at Wednesday evening's banquet.
Trump did not follow Xi with a toast of his own. This was the same famously outspoken president, who in a winding speech in Davos, had declared that the U.S. must get Greenland .
Yet on Wednesday night in China, Trump wasn't the one holding the microphone.

articles.content_orig:
Siddharth 18 November 2026
Apple is reportedly planning a major redesign for its 20th-anniversary iPhone 20 Pro lineup next year, with quad-curved displays and several other improvements. A new leak has now revealed more details about the upcoming models.
Tipster Ice Universe shared the latest details about the 20th-anniversary iPhones on X, claiming that Apple is developing four models for next year.
Two of the models will feature flat cover glass, while the other two will sport the much-rumored quad-curved design. Apple has reportedly been developing the new design for around three years, making several revisions along the way.
According to Ice Universe, early prototypes had deeper curves, which were later toned down. The tipster also claims that the quad-curved glass shown in a recently leaked video belonged to an early prototype.
The models with quad-curved glass are said to have 1mm bezels. However, the curvature is said to make them almost invisible when viewed straight on. Ice Universe also claims that industry insiders are more excited about the upcoming anniversary iPhones than the recently launched iPhone Duo .

articles.title_orig: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
articles.title_zh: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
articles.content_orig:
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.
If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.
So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?
In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.
He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.
Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track , and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.
Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.
Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.
But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.
Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".
Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.
She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.
Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.
She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.
The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.
Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.
He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.
Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.
He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".
Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.
Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.
Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.
He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.
Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.
Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.
He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.
His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.
Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.
But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.
Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.
He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.
The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.
Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.
McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.
He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6: PS5 vs PS5 Pro, Xbox Series X and Series S: Which Console Plays Best?
articles.title_zh: GTA 6: PS5 vs PS5 Pro, Xbox Series X and Series S: Which Console Plays Best?
articles.content_orig:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is here - and that means we can finally share the full details of how the game performs on each console platform: base PS5, PS5 Pro, Xbox Series X and Series S.
We've already covered GTA 6's visuals in detail , focusing on the top-end experience on PS5 Pro, but the game's performance and fidelity can vary significantly depending on your platform of choice. The PlayStation and Xbox releases use different upscalers, for example, while the PS5 Pro release adds extra ray tracing effects. The Series S version is perhaps the most interesting of all, as it has to cram an extraordinary visual burden onto the weakest current-gen hardware - and more or less pulls it off, despite some noticeable cutbacks.
This article compares the game on every platform based on over 100 hours of testing across all four versions by John and Oliver, focusing on image quality, visual features and performance.
First, let's touch on resolution. The game runs at 2560x1440 (1440p) resolution on PS5, PS5 Pro and Xbox Series X, with no immediate signs of dynamic resolution scaling.
On PS5 Pro, this is upscaled to 4K using PSSR, the Pro's bespoke AI temporal upscaler. PS5 and Xbox Series X instead get a spatial upscale to 4K using Rockstar's in-house TAA. The game therefore doesn't use temporal upscaling - such as QSSR on PS5 or FSR on Series X - and appears visually softer as a result. However, the decision does make sense .
The Series S is the odd one out here, with an internal resolution of 720p, temporally upscaled to approximately 1080p using FSR 4. From what we understand, this is the first shipping game on Series consoles to use the new upscaler .
All platforms target a 30fps frame-rate, a rarity for a current-gen game, but given the huge scale and intense simulation elements, the design makes sense . There's no option for a 40fps or 60fps mode on any platform.
As an aside, Xbox consoles can run the game in a 120Hz VRR container as an OS-level feature, which allows for a slightly smoother experience. PlayStation users don't have a 120Hz option, and while you can force VRR on, the system-level VRR only operates above 48fps and doesn't support low frame-rate compensation, so this does nothing in a 30fps title.
In terms of performance, the PS5 Pro offers the smoothest experience, with a consistent 30fps experience through around 75 hours of standard play in our testing. However, it is possible to experience short drops to a minimum of 24fps when destroying vehicles with the grenade launcher, but the frame-rate tends to recover quickly.
The base PS5 and Series X use the same 30fps target, but hold it a little more loosely, often flicking between 30fps and the high 20s during traversal, combat and other more challenging scenes. Returning to the same vehicle destruction hotspot, the frame-rate remains in the mid-30s while the carnage is unfolding, and only recovers when we leave the area. Again, it's possible for frame-rates to dip into the low 20s at the worst case.
Series S offers the loosest 30fps lock, with large portions of the game playing out at frame-rates from the mid to high 20s. Again, it's possible to depress the frame-rate to around 20fps with vehicular destruction. The other consoles do a credible job of hitting 30fps, but Series S often lies in a 25-30fps no-man's-land.
Note that, distinct from frame-rate, the game featured some animation update rate unsteadiness in pre-release footage (and our early testing on Xbox Series consoles). Thankfully, this long-standing RAGE engine issue seems to have been fixed in patches prior to launch, and animations now play out with consistent frame pacing.
Finally, input lag is similar to other Rockstar 30fps titles, like Red Dead Redemption 2. We measured around 180ms of end-to-end camera movement latency on Series X, including a wireless controller and around 10ms of display latency. This didn't seem to change substantially across 60Hz, 120Hz and 120Hz VRR. This is similar to RDR 2 and GTA 5 Enhanced, though input response is perceptually a bit better in GTA 6.
While all versions of the game - PS5, PS5 Pro, Series X, Series S - use ray-traced global illumination (RTGI) and ray-traced reflections, only the PS5 Pro version additionally supports ray-traced shadows. On other platforms, less consistent shadow maps are used, though these do support variable penumbra and have a high-resolution appearance.
Note that the RT reflections on all consoles are part of a hybrid approach, with screen-space reflections (SSR) layered in.
The Series S version is surprisingly feature-complete compared to the PS5 and Series X versions, supporting strand-based hair and the two RT effects, but it does come with some cutbacks. Most notably, lighting is lower precision overall and RT reflections are softer, lower-res and sometimes miss details. Shadows also appear visually degraded, with lower resolution shadowmaps and some absent cutscene self-shadows.
Additionally, driving at high speed through the game world results in more noticeable pop-in. Other minor downgrades include muddier textures at oblique angles, lower-res volumetric clouds, flatter water, lower-res hair and facial hair, and lower resolution depth of field effects.
Despite these necessary cutbacks, due to the Series S console's more limited memory and cut-down GPU, the overall visual feature set is still similar to Xbox Series X and PS5. Thankfully, the full-fat CPU and SSD on the Series S mean that the scale and scope of Leonida isn't affected.
It's worth bearing in mind that the nature of the game make it hard to nail down absolutely every change, especially as John played only on PS5 and PS5 Pro, while Oliver played only on Xbox Series X and Series S. We'll have more direct cross-platform comparisons in future content.
In terms of visual features and performance, the PS5 Pro version is the best option available, with solid frame-rates, 4K-like image quality and a noticeable visual upgrade thanks to ray-traced shadows. However, the game looks and plays well on base PS5 and Xbox Series X as well, despite occasional minor frame-rate drops during regular play and a softer 1440p image. The Series S version of the game is the hardest to recommend, with consistent frame-rate drops to the mid-20s, a 1080p output resolution and a long list of visual cutbacks, though the overall character of the game's visuals still shines through.
For more, why not read our full GTA 6 tech review ?

articles.title_orig: Bill Gurley says giving away AI is Google's 'No. 1' move against Anthropic
articles.title_zh: Bill Gurley says giving away AI is Google's 'No. 1' move against Anthropic
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Bill Gurley , the venture capitalist behind an early bet on Uber ( UBER ), has an idea for how Google could slow Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) down: Give the AI away.
Gurley, a general partner at Benchmark, told Deirdre Bosa Live on Monday that Alphabet's ( GOOGL ) Google should use free AI to keep Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) and OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) from pulling away. Anthropic prices its IPO Wednesday and begins trading Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT .
"If Google recognizes that Anthropic ... and OpenAI maybe are getting escape velocity away from them, it is the No. 1 thing they should go do ... bar none," he said.
Gurley calls it playing defense. Open-weight models, which anyone can download, run and change for free, keep one company from locking up a market. Google did it with Kubernetes "when they were worried about Amazon and AWS," he said, and with Android "when they were worried about Apple having a monopoly in phones."
The catch? "We're not seeing those actions from Google."
Free models already do most of the work. On OpenRouter, a marketplace developers use to reach hundreds of AI models, seven of the 10 most-used models last week came from Chinese labs and are free to download. DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash alone processed about 77 trillion tokens, the basic units of text that AI models read and write. That's more than the other nine combined.
Duolingo ( DUOL ) CEO Luis von Ahn told Yahoo Finance last week that open models cut the cost of each AI video call to less than a cent from about 30 cents. "The vast majority of our usage of AI will be in open-weight models pretty soon," he said.
The money flows the other way. Closed models handled 28% of OpenRouter's tokens in mid-September but collected 73% of the spending, according to its September report . Similarly, Apple's ( AAPL ) iPhone accounted for about a fifth of phones sold in the second quarter but generated nearly half of revenue, according to Counterpoint Research.
Price is a big reason. Anthropic lists Claude Opus 5.5, its most-used model, at about 27 times what DeepSeek charges for its own. And while 39 companies sell DeepSeek's model on OpenRouter, nobody sells Claude Opus for less than Anthropic does. As Gurley put it, "The marginal price is going to equal marginal cost."
Gurley also called Anthropic's choice to write off model training costs right away, rather than over years, "pretty amazing," adding, "it's still profitable, really high gross margin."
"Anthropic — just reading through the S-1 — I think it's the most impressive business I've ever reviewed," Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang on Friday.
OpenRouter tracks developers, not the ChatGPT or Claude apps. And Android cut both ways. It protected Google, but Apple kept collecting.
Gurley's worry is Washington. He said Anthropic's lobbying effort is "probably unprecedented for a company of their age or size," and he sees it as a push for regulatory capture , meaning rules shaped by the companies they govern. In AI, that could mean rules that favor closed labs over open models.
He still gives Anthropic its due. "It is remarkable what they've done," he said. "I tip my hat to them. I just wish they weren't lobbying so hard."
Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication.
Jared Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance. Follow him on X at @SPYJared or email him at jaredblikre@yahooinc.com .

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before Senate banking committee, Chairman Scott says
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before Senate banking committee, Chairman Scott says
articles.content_orig:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee, panel Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., said on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also agreed to testify, Scott said. The agreements to appear voluntarily come as pressure builds on Capitol Hill to investigate Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy, which led to his ouster at the chipmaker he founded.
"They both have agreed," Scott said. "We will hopefully have this done before Christmas."
Huang reached an agreement on Tuesday with the chairmen of three House committees for a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1 jointly before the three panels. Scott had asked Huang to appear publicly in the Senate.
A spokesperson for the banking committee did not immediately respond to questions about when Huang and Lutnick would testify. In initial letters to the pair, Scott requested Huang appear on Dec. 3 and Lutnick appear on Dec. 10.
Scott said the appearances will provide the committee with "more information about what they knew, when they knew it and why they didn't do something about it."
"Nvidia seemed to have fairly lax controls, and I want to know how much of the relationship with Alice [Huang] impacted Nvidia's unwillingness or inability, or frankly, just blindness to Megaspeed's providing access to China of the most advanced chipset," Scott said of Jensen Huang's testimony.
The outgoing banking committee chair also homed in on Lutnick, calling for answers as to why the commerce secretary did not act after being warned about Megaspeed — the Singaporean company where the alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, was an executive. Nvidia sold its chips to Megaspeed, which U.S. investigators suspect of diverting them to China.
"They were warned as early as March of this year, several months ago, that Megaspeed should be on the 'entity list,'" Scott said, referring to a Commerce Department list of companies the U.S. views as national security risks. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security "didn't do it, Howard didn't do it, we want to know why."
Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have been embroiled in an intra-administration battle as the fallout from the Huang affair grows. Bessent on CNBC on Friday appeared to blame Lutnick for a lack of action on Megaspeed.
"You will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said, referring to Commerce and noting his department has long supported imposing restrictions on Megaspeed.
A spokesperson for Huang declined to comment on Scott's announcement that he has agreed to appear.
Huang's upcoming appearances are likely just the start of the embattled former CEO's problems on Capitol Hill. Democrats will take control of Congress in January and have demanded sweeping investigations into the affair and Huang's cozy relationship with President Donald Trump .
The House Energy and Commerce Committee asked interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress for a briefing no later than Dec. 2 on the company's chip exports and information about the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang. The panel also asked Lutnick and a top deputy to appear to discuss chip export controls. The Wall Street Journal first reported the letters to Kress and Lutnick, and a committee spokesperson confirmed the report to CNBC.
— Megan Cassella and Ashlee Trujillo contributed to this report.
